news.title: Kamala Harris' Chances of Beating Newsom and AOC in New 2028 Poll
news.text: Former Vice President Kamala Harris has maintained a sizable early lead over two of the most closely watched potential Democratic contenders for 2028, according to a new Rasmussen Reports poll. The survey of likely voters found Harris with 37 percent support, well ahead of California Governor Gavin Newsom at 14 percent and New York Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at 9 percent. Harris’ number also marks an improvement from May, when she registered 34 percent support with the pollster, suggesting that her position at the top of the early Democratic field has strengthened rather than weakened. The poll comes as other national surveys show mixed frontrunners. Early polls have gained significance as potential contenders for the 2028 presidential election begin to emerge. Even with the election still years away, polling offers insight into potential candidate viability, voter sentiment and evolving party dynamics, particularly after the pivotal 2024 election cycle. Harris told the Reverend Al Sharpton earlier this year that she is "thinking about it," when asked if she's considering a 2028 run. What To Know The biggest challenge to Harris’ lead appears to be the sheer distance between her and the rest of the field. Newsom is currently her closest rival, but he trails Harris by 23 percentage points. Ocasio-Cortez, meanwhile, has slipped from 11 percent in May to 9 percent, moving her into a tie for fourth place with Arizona Senator Mark Kelly. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg sits between Newsom and Ocasio-Cortez at 10 percent. The numbers indicate that, at least for now, Harris has established a clear advantage among the voters Rasmussen identified as likely Democratic primary voters. Grant Davis Reeher, a professor of political science at Syracuse University, told Newsweek via email on Monday, "It is interesting that AOC has fallen, given the rising star of democratic socialism in Democratic primaries. Maybe there is some buyer’s remorse that’s being reflected in that poll. It’s still very early, and my hunch remains that Kamala Harris’s support is soft (although she has a core of staunch supporters). "I would expect to see some more formal or more serious declarations of interest after the mid-terms. We’ll have a better sense of the depth of the reaction against Trump since 2025, and whether the left wing of the Democratic Party can win general elections." Harris’ strongest advantage comes from several important Democratic constituencies. The poll finds that Black voters are particularly likely to participate in the Democratic primary, while Harris draws her strongest support from Black voters and other minority voters. She also performs particularly well among younger Democratic primary voters: 53 percent of those under 40 who are likely Democratic primary voters say they favor Harris. By comparison, her support falls sharply among voters 65 and older, where Mark Kelly is the stronger preference. That age divide could become significant if the Democratic field changes substantially before voting begins. At the same time, the poll should not be interpreted as proof that Harris is on track to win the 2028 Democratic nomination, as no candidate has formally announced their intentions to run. The survey shows that all other potential candidates received single digits, including Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff and Illinois Governor J.B. Pritzker. The poll shows that 2 percent would vote for another candidate, while 7 percent are not sure. The survey was conducted from August 2 to August 4, 2026, and questioned 504 voters who said they were more likely to participate in the Democratic presidential primary. The poll's margin of error is 3 percent. For now, it appears that Harris has the strongest early position among the candidates tested, while Newsom remains the closest challenger and Ocasio-Cortez has lost some ground. Whether Harris' lead survives the scrutiny of a presidential campaign is a much bigger question, but if the Democratic primary were held today, this poll suggests Harris would enter the contest with a substantial advantage over both Newsom and Ocasio-Cortez. What Other Polls Show A McLaughlin & Associates poll taken last month shows Harris with 28 percent, Newsom with 17 percent, Ocasio-Cortez with 10 percent and Buttigieg with 8 percent. The survey shows that 14 percent were undecided. The poll was taken from July 15 to July 21, 2026, among 472 respondents. An Emerson College Poll last month showed Buttigieg with 19 percent and Newsom with 17 percent. Ossoff had 13 percent, Ocasio-Cortez had 13 percent, Harris had 8 percent, Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear had 7 percent, Shapiro landed 5 percent and Pritzker had 3 percent. Representative Ro Khanna landed 2 percent, 3 percent would pick someone else, and 13 percent were undecided. The poll was conducted from July 19 to July 20, 2026, among 574 respondents and had a margin of error of 4 percent. The Rasmussen and the Emerson College polls paint markedly different pictures of the Democratic field, largely because of Harris's standing. Rasmussen found the former vice president commanding 37 percent support among likely Democratic primary voters, while an Emerson College poll conducted two weeks earlier measured Harris at 8 percent. Yet support for several other potential contenders, including Gavin Newsom, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Josh Shapiro, was broadly similar across both surveys, suggesting methodological differences rather than a dramatic shift in the race may explain much of the gap. What's Next While no major 2028 candidates have formally declared, presidential hopefuls typically begin testing runs, building donor networks and visiting early-voting states shortly after the midterms. Formal campaign announcements are expected throughout 2027, ahead of the first primary contests in early 2028. Key dates: Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: Even with the election still years away, polling offers insight into potential candidate viability and voter sentiment.
news.author: Anna Commander

news.title: The bleak reason Max Miller didn’t drop out of his race
news.text:
As of 4 p.m. on Monday, Ohio Rep. Max Miller officially passed the deadline for being replaced by party leaders on the ballot following domestic abuse allegations and calls from a handful of Republican senators to step down from office as he seeks re-election. (He has denied the allegations.) 

And so the GOP is stuck with him in November. 

But there are few signs that the Republican Party as a whole is all that broken up about it. Despite the severity of the allegations against Miller — which include claims that Miller threw hot water on his ex-wife, held a gun to her head, and may have broken their young daughter's collarbone — the party did not pile on to the longtime Trump devotee. (An investigation into claims of child abuse found there was not enough evidence to bring charge.)

The foremost example of how accusations of violence against women are tolerable on the right is Trump himself.

In the days leading up to the deadline, President Donald Trump praised Miller as a “good person” and said he wanted “to let the families figure that out.” House Speaker Mike Johnson said he preferred a House ethics committee investigation play out (which can be a slow and drawn-out process), while Senate Majority Leader John Thune called it a “House matter” and a “family issue.” While some GOP senators did express concerns about the allegations, their numbers did not come close to achieving a majority view within their caucus. 

The objections to Miller in Washington were so restrained that right-wing pundit Erick Erickson wondered last week on X why Miller wasn’t getting “the Graham Platner treatment,” a reference to how the Democratic senate candidate in Maine dropped out of his race after a sexual assault allegation resulted in a swift and widespread backlash within the Democratic Party, including from his most influential backer, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt. (Platner denied the allegation, which came after other allegations of “toxic” behavior toward romantic partners which he also denied.)

The answer is simple, and rather bleak: The MAGA right is historically tolerant of accusations of abusive behavior.

As Politico reported, a Politico poll conducted in July in partnership with Public First, which surveyed over 2,000 U.S. adults online, found that “Trump’s MAGA supporters are the most loyal of any group of voters — with majorities saying they would stick by GOP candidates confronted with an array of scandals, from a DUI conviction or accepting lobbyist gifts to more serious accusations including domestic violence, sexual assault and antisemitic social media posts.” 

The poll specifically found that 72% of self-described MAGA Trump voters said they would stick with a Republican candidate accused of domestic violence. That’s considerably higher than the 61% overall share of Trump 2024 voters who would back such a Republican candidate, and far more than the 39% of 2024 Kamala Harris voters who said they would remain supportive of a Democrat accused of domestic violence. (Note: The margin of error for the overall survey is ±2.16 percentage points, but subgroups have higher margins of error.)

Part of the explanation may be a tolerance or affinity for abusive behavior, especially from men, considering that the GOP under Trump has become a bastion of strongman politics, bald imperialism, reactionary conceptions of masculinity, friendly toward political violence and, in some instances, has charged human traffickers. Another part of the explanation could be a generalized distrust of institutions and a belief that allegations that surface in the mainstream media are attached to some shadowy conspiracy against MAGA politicos. Whatever the reason, it’s disturbing. 

A recent Washington Post report published last week supports the idea that Miller may not have fallen out with the GOP base. The Post interviewed dozens of voters across his district, finding that, among those who knew of the allegations, they were “largely wary of wading into what they considered a family matter and reluctant to abandon Miller.”

Of course the foremost example of how accusations of violence against women are tolerable on the right is Trump himself. The president has been accused of sexual misconduct by dozens of women, and it didn’t stop him from getting elected twice, or hurt his reputation with his core base. (Trump has denied the allegations.)

Miller even cited Trump’s behavior as inspiration to stay in the race. In response to a list of accusations of abuse from three women during an interview with CNN’s Jake Tapper, Miller denied the accusations, saying, “In 2016, when President Donald J. Trump faced the most extreme allegations in the world that hit him day after day after day, and people in the media, very much like yourself and others, said that he would have no shot at winning, that he should not be the president of the United States. But guess what? He stayed in, and he was resilient.”

Notably, Miller didn’t say that all the allegations against Trump were necessarily false. Rather, he observed, and seemed to celebrate, that despite them, Trump was able to prevail. He seems to believe that the same applies to him — and he could be right.

news.title: Lefties like AOC need to answer some questions before we move on from ‘Woke 1’
news.text:
Remember the early 2020s when cancel culture ran rampant, defunding police was a standard position on the left and we were all supposed to fall in line with their bad ideas, or else?

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez wants us to pretend it all went away.

AOC took to “This Week with Jonathan Karl” on ABC to defend Francesca Hong, the latest Democratic Socialist star, running for governor of Wisconsin.

In 2020, Hong said Thanksgiving should be canceled, claiming it’s “a time that’s incredibly painful for people” in her community.

Now that she wants to get elected, Hong suddenly called Thanksgiving her “favorite holiday.”

AOC argued that Hong has “moved away” from some of her more controversial positions then giggled that she agreed with NYC Councilman Chi Ossé, who had said, “Woke 1 was crazyyyy.”

Tee-hee, woke 1, you guys! We were so goofy and silly, what with destroying the lives of anyone who mildly disagreed with us. 

Forget about all the crazy things we said! Focus on the cleaned up versions of those positions that we’re spouting now!

But before we move on, perhaps a few follow-up questions:

What era of “woke” are we in now? 2? 5? Which parts in particular does the left regret? 

Is it stuff like a New York Times columnist saying the cartoon character Pepé Le Pew “normalized rape culture” or when we finally solved racism by getting rid of Aunt Jemima on the pancake syrup?

Was it the 57 genders, the biological boys dominating in girls’ sports and the girls having to shut up about it, the astronomical number of teens who suddenly declared themselves “non-binary” and sometimes participated in life-altering and dangerous medical interventions in a futile attempt to change their gender?

Does no one want to get rid of police departments or prisons anymore?

The left only stopped some of this nonsense because the American people made them stop, largely by electing President Donald Trump for a second term.

Trump’s most powerful ad noted that Kamala Harris, now somehow a “moderate” in a Democratic Party being taken over by communists, wanted free sex changes for illegal immigrant criminals. It seemed so outlandish that it couldn’t be true.

It was true.

The left has realized how absurd their ideas sound to everyday Americans, and they’re trying to massage what they really believe.

As AOC admitted, “I think that when we talk about crime today, it’s fundamentally different than the way that we talked about crime, in bringing crime down, right? I think that during lockdown, of course, rhetoric in that time is not rhetoric that we would use today.”

In June 2020, when NYC proposed cutting NYPD’s budget by $1.5 billion, AOC didn’t think that went far enough. “Defunding police means defunding police. It does not mean budget tricks or funny math.”

A month later she said “Crime is a symptom of a diseased society that neglects its most marginalized people, and we do not solve that problem with police.”

But it wasn’t just a symptom of the lockdowns, as she portrays it today. Before COVID, back in 2019, AOC tweeted that “we need to have a real conversation about decarceration & prison abolition in this country.”

She was for getting rid of police departments and prisons. Are we supposed to just forget what she said?

And, more importantly, are we suppose to really believe she doesn’t think that anymore — or she’s just savvy enough to say otherwise?

There is no Woke 2. It’s exactly the same as Woke 1, just better focus-grouped.

Karol Markowicz is the host of the “Karol Markowicz Show” and “Normally” podcasts.
news.summary: Remember the early 2020s when cancel culture ran rampant, defunding police was a standard position on the left and we were all supposed to fall in line with their bad ideas, or else?

news.title: You can’t erase woke
news.text:
Hong did not address a more fundamental question: Isn’t it a problem that she ever believed those things? Hong was in her early 30s when she expressed the views listed above. Now approaching 40, she has been slow to back away from them, and only under pressure. Isn’t that a problem?

The progressive answer to that question came over the weekend from far-left superstar Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY). “I have a local city councilman that has this saying: Woke 1 was crazy,” she said with a laugh on ABC News’s This Week Sunday. “And I think that what’s important is that we have to assess what a candidate is saying now.”

That is what Ocasio-Cortez wants, and what Hong wants, and what lots of other socialists and progressives want, but it is fortunately not the way the political system works. Things a candidate has said in the past, especially in the recent past, mean something. They should face questions about them.

Graham Platner, who won the Democratic nomination for Senate in Maine, had a ton of social media posts to run away from. None of them forced him out of the race; that happened only after he was accused of sexual assault. In Michigan, Abdul el Sayed, or Abdulrahman Mohamed el Sayed, as Republicans call him, also had a lot of posts to live down — which he successfully did, winning the Democratic nomination for Senate.

Neither candidate faced a particularly adversarial press when it came to those old posts. They were running in Democratic primaries where there were less likely to be impassioned arguments about such views. For el Sayed, and for Hong if she wins, the situation will be different in the general election campaign, where they will be running against Republicans who will be more than happy to point out their statements from a few years ago.

Kamala Harris got to experience that in the 2024 presidential race. Remember that Harris ran for the 2020 Democratic nomination for president. She was a terrible candidate and dropped out in December 2019. But she left a record of ridiculous comments that came back to haunt her in 2024.

“If there was a bad idea, she embraced it,” this newsletter noted earlier this year. “Green New Deal, Medicare for all, mandatory assault weapon buybacks, amnesty — the whole lot. (Harris also said she was ‘open’ to the idea of packing the Supreme Court.)”

Then there was the legendary moment in the 2024 presidential debate in which Trump accused Harris of “wanting to do transgender operations on illegal aliens that are in prison.” Some Harris supporters reacted with outrage — surely Trump was making up a crazy charge like that! But no, Trump was correct. Harris had actually made the pledge in writing in a 2019 questionnaire for the American Civil Liberties Union. Her views from five years earlier hurt her a lot in 2024.

Now, Ocasio-Cortez says the important thing is “to assess what a candidate is saying now.” But why not take what that candidate said just a few years ago into account? “I don’t love this idea that nothing anyone said or did in 2019-2020 counts,” tweeted left-leaning writer Matthew Yglesias. “Like it’s fine as a sociological observation, but I want political leaders who keep their heads even in the face of dumb fads.”

Francesca Hong did not do that. Abdul el Sayed did not do that. Kamala Harris did not do that. And woke was indeed crazy. So now, it’s entirely reasonable for voters to ask why those candidates believed it so fervently.
news.summary: YOU CAN’T ERASE WOKE. This political season, like the last couple, has featured Democratic candidates not only running for office but running away from things they said from 2019 to 2021. The latest is Francesca Hong, the somewhat loopy front-runner for the Democratic nomination for governor of Wisconsin. In the last few days, Hong has walked back […]

news.title: Does Jackson County need a weaker executive? One legislator thinks so
news.text:
The stunning indictment of Jackson County Executive Phil LeVota last week marked another illustrative example of the position’s outsized power, according to one top lawmaker.

Jackson County has had a string of scandals rock the executive’s office prior to federal officials accusing LeVota of orchestrating a bribery scheme.

Prior to LeVota, Frank White was pushed out of office in an overwhelming recall vote last year.

Former County Executive Mike Sanders, White’s predecessor, was indicted and convicted of conspiracy to commit wire fraud. Before Sanders, former Executive Katheryn Shields was accused of wire fraud, but was cleared of the charges.

“We’re talking about 30 years of Jackson County history, and I firmly believe that our county executive under our current structure of government has too much authority, and that maybe that’s where the problems are emanating from,” said Jackson County 6th District Legislator Sean Smith.

Smith said that the repeated scandals could deter qualified candidates from running for county executive in the future.

“The more of these scandals that happen, the fewer people are going to want to be county executive,” Smith said. “I really think it’s important for people to start to think about why this keeps happening.”

Smith clarified that LeVota deserves his day in court, and that he believes LeVota has “done some great things for the county.”

He also has questions about the indictment, and if what occurred is a crime. He likened LeVota’s alleged promise of a job to “Individual 1” in the indictment to President Donald Trump’s hiring Robert Kennedy Jr. as Health and Human Services Secretary after Kennedy dropped his campaign for president and endorsed Trump.

On Thursday, LeVota proclaimed his innocence and vowed to stay in office as the case proceeds. At a news conference, he said an unnamed “Individual 1” in the indictment was Jackson County Legislator DaRon McGee.

“As I read it, I got a hint of ‘person one’ seeming to try to lock him down, and you know, like unnaturally so,” Smith said. “It’s a little hard to see where this is very different from the situation I just described with Trump, or name the same situation with Biden bringing Kamala Harris on as his vice president.”

The Star reached out to members of the Jackson County Legislature for comment, but only one other responded when this article was published.

Jackson County 1st District Legislator Manny Abarca, reached by phone Thursday, said he was stunned by the news of LeVota’s indictment. He flatly said it was illustrative of “more chaos in Jackson County.”

“Unfortunately, we’ve not even dealt with the potential bribery attempt from my end,” he said. “So I think there’s more to come.”

Last month, Abarca said he was offered a $10,000 campaign contribution in exchange for a favorable vote on county business.

Stacy Lake, the Democratic candidate for Jackson County executive, declined to comment specifically, but said she “recognizes the seriousness of the indictment” through a spokesperson.

“She will be closely monitoring the situation as it unfolds, but we must allow the charges to follow the proper course through the courts,” said Carter Taylor, a spokesperson for Lake.

Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway, a Republican, said her office was not involved in the investigation or indictment, but commended the U.S. Attorney’s Office and FBI for addressing public corruption.

“We support efforts to uphold the merit system, root out corruption, and ensure that public officials are held to the highest standards of accountability,” said Colbey Stosberg, a spokesperson for the Missouri attorney general’s office.

The Star’s Kacen Bayless contributed to this report.
news.author: Jack Harvel

news.title: Jeffrey Toobin Lays Out Democrats' Doomsday Scenario for Midterms
news.text: Jeffrey Toobin, former chief legal analyst for CNN, has covered elections and the courts for three decades, from the O.J. Simpson trial to the Supreme Court. But before he began reporting his latest essay for The New York Times, he says, he knew almost nothing about how the roll of the House of Representatives actually gets compiled. "I am pleased to say that before I started reporting this piece, I knew nothing about this," Toobin told Politics and Culture Director Carlo Versano in an interview on Newsweek's The 1600 podcast. Neither, he found, did most members of Congress. The process, Toobin said, has historically been "ministerial" and "automatic," carried out by an official almost nobody outside Washington could name. That is starting to change. Watch Here: The 1600 Podcast Full Episode The Clerk Scenario Toobin's Times op-ed called What's the Worst Thing Trump Can Do in the Midterms? traces a disaster scenario relayed to him by New York Democratic Representative Joe Morelle, ranking member of the House Administration Committee. Under federal law, the clerk of the House compiles the roll of newly elected members after states certify their results, typically in late November or early December. That roll is what gets used to seat the new Congress on January 3. The current clerk, Kevin McCumber, was appointed in 2023 by then-Speaker Kevin McCarthy but previously worked under Speaker Nancy Pelosi and is widely seen as nonpartisan. The fear, Toobin said, is that if Democrats win a narrow House majority in November and President Donald Trump declares the results fraudulent, he could press House Speaker Mike Johnson to fire McCumber and install a replacement willing to produce a different roll. "The worry that Democrats like Joe Morelle, the congressman I spoke to at some length, the worry is Mike Johnson will fire Kevin McCumber and install someone of his choosing, presumably a MAGA ally who will compile a different roll," Toobin said. Johnson has the legal authority to remove the clerk unilaterally, Toobin said, though a permanent replacement would need to be confirmed by a majority vote of the outgoing House. Morelle believes that vote might fail, given the number of retiring or reluctant Republicans. But that leaves an unresolved question: What powers does an acting clerk have in the meantime? "That's where I think the existing law is particularly unclear," Toobin said. "I don't have a resolution, but I certainly flag the issue." Why the Courts Might Stay Out of It Unlike the Senate, which never fully adjourns, the House ceases to exist under the Constitution at noon January 3 unless a new one is sworn in. That hard deadline is what makes the clerk fight dangerous, Toobin said, because any delay could leave the chamber in limbo. Toobin cautioned that the courts may not ride to the rescue. Federal judges have long applied what is known as the political question doctrine, treating the internal workings of Congress as off-limits to judicial review. "There is at least some possibility that if either side went to court to try to resolve this issue of what are the powers of an acting clerk or what are grounds in which a new clerk can be appointed, that the federal courts would say, look, this is an internal matter for a coordinate branch of government," Toobin said. He drew a sharper distinction for state-level certification fights, which he said courts have handled more decisively, sometimes removing officials who refuse to certify results. "This is not a political question issue," Toobin said. "This is an issue of compliance with state law." Troops at the Polls, and a Mystery Over Mail Ballots Toobin also weighed in on tactics that are already public, starting with the prospect of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents or National Guard troops stationed near polling places. He framed it less as a legal question than a psychological one, aimed at discouraging turnout rather than stopping fraud. "If you are an American citizen who is married to someone who is not an American citizen, do you want to call attention to yourself by having your ID checked by an ICE official," Toobin said. "Voting is protected by the Constitution. So the idea that we should have to run a gauntlet of military or paramilitary to vote is anathema." Toobin connected it to a broader discomfort with government overreach that used to cut across party lines. "This used to be like a Republican thing, not wanting the law enforcement and the military all up in your business," Versano said. Toobin agreed, adding that even the administration's stated rationale, rooting out fraud, does not hold up cleanly when applied to Trump's other obsession: mail-in voting. Trump has fought to limit mail balloting, including a directive to the U.S. Postal Service to restrict delivery in states that withhold voter data from the federal government, a move a federal judge has already blocked. But Toobin pointed out that the partisan benefit of mail voting is not even settled. "To this day, it's unclear which party is helped by mail-in voting," Toobin said. "Going back a decade or two, it was Republicans who all wanted mail-in voting, and some people still think Republicans benefit more by mail-in voting. So some of this stuff is not only pernicious, it is just mysterious." The Cure Is a Landslide Toobin said the entire scenario only becomes plausible if the House majority is razor thin, under roughly 10 seats. A wave election in either direction would render the fight moot. "If the Democrats pick up 20, 30, 40 seats, as has often been the case in midterm wave elections, then I think there is nothing to worry about," Toobin said. He also pointed to a related, less discussed erosion of political norms: mid-decade redistricting, set off by Texas' Republican-led remap and California's Democratic response. Toobin called it a norm as significant as the certification fights, warning that Congress could be redrawn every two years going forward. "Is that a system that anyone, including the Republicans, want?" he asked. When asked why Trump refuses to accept his 2020 loss, Toobin traced it partly to Trump's relationship with the late lawyer Roy Cohn, whose rule, he said, was "you never admit that you lost." Toobin flagged Iowa and Texas as the Senate races he is watching most closely, and named Ohio, where polling shows Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown ahead by as much as 8 points, and Florida as states where Trump could still intervene. He was also blunt about Johnson. "I think he is a political creature of Donald Trump whose views begin and end with what Trump wants to do," Toobin said. "I don't think he's an institutionalist at all." And he was self-deprecating about his own record, admitting his worst recent call was expecting former Vice President Kamala Harris to win in 2024. "I have really tried to get out of the business of predicting sure outcomes," Toobin said, "not just because I'm wrong, but because it's just not helpful." news.summary: Jeffrey Toobin says Democrats fear Trump could fire the House clerk to rewrite the midterm results.

news.title: Peggy Flanagan's Chances Against Angie Craig: Final Minnesota Primary Polls
news.text: Lieutenant Governor Peggy Flanagan and Representative Angie Craig are engaged in a competitive race heading into Tuesday's Minnesota Democratic Senate primary, another key electoral test for progressives after a wave of recent victories. Flanagan is viewed as the progressive pick in the race to succeed Democratic Senator Tina Smith, who is retiring at the end of the current term, while Craig is seen as the more moderate Democratic candidate. Progressives are on a winning streak, having won primaries in states like Michigan, New York and Colorado, and Minnesota presents them with another opportunity to elect a more left-leaning candidate in a state that is considered to lean toward Democrats. Minnesota backed former Vice President Kamala Harris by about four points in 2024, and Democrats are viewed as having an advantage in this year’s midterms due to a more favorable national environment driven by President Donald Trump’s declining national approval rating. But it’s not an overwhelmingly Democratic state, so the question of electability has been central in the primary. Flanagan's supporters believe a left-leaning state should elect a more progressive senator, such as Smith, who has endorsed Flanagan. They have raised concern about Craig’s past votes on immigration issues. However, Craig supporters note that she has a proven track record of winning in a competitive district, having flipped a Trump district in the 2018 midterms in the Twin Cities suburbs, and that Flanagan could be vulnerable to Republican attacks about the way Governor Tim Walz’s administration has handled a fraud scandal in the state. Mara Kunin, campaign manager for Angie Craig for Minnesota, wrote in a statement that polls show Craig surging. “National and state Republicans are making a serious play for this Senate seat and primary voters understand that we can’t risk putting up a weak candidate in the general election. Whether it’s standing up to Donald Trump or keeping Minnesota’s Senate seat blue, Angie is leading on the issues DFLers [supporters of the Minnesota Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party] care most about while Peggy Flanagan’s numbers continue to plummet,” Kunin wrote. Newsweek also reached out to Flanagan’s campaign for comment via email. Peggy Flanagan vs. Angie Craig: What Final Polls Show The latest polls of Minnesotans show a competitive race between Flanagan and Craig in the final days before Election Day. A SurveyUSA poll, sponsored by KSTP-TV, showed Craig with a 2-point lead, 42 percent to 40 percent. It surveyed 578 likely voters from July 29 to August 4. But a Public Policy Polling review, which surveyed 672 likely voters on July 23 and July 24, showed Flanagan up 14 points, 46 percent to 32 percent, with 22 percent undecided. It was sponsored by the Democratic Lieutenant Governors Association, which has supported Flanagan. An earlier SurveyUSA poll, sponsored by KSTP-TV, KAAL-TV and WDIO-TV, pointed to a close race, with each candidate receiving 40 percent support. It was conducted from July 15 to July 20 among 513 likely voters. David Schultz, professor of political science at Hamline University, told Newsweek that youth turnout is a major question for the outcome of the primary. “Even when younger voters tell pollsters that they intend to vote, their actual turnout is often substantially lower. This matters because a core part of Flanagan's support is likely to come from younger voters, including students,” he said. He noted that in Michigan, progressive candidate Abdul El-Sayed held a larger polling lead but ultimately eked out a victory over centrist Representative Haley Stevens. “Maybe that is partly a story about bad polling, but it is also a story about turnout. We know that people under 30 generally have dramatically lower turnout rates than people over 30,” he said. Immigration Is Key Issue Flanagan has been critical of Craig’s stance on immigration in Minnesota, where the issue may hit home for many voters. The North Star State became the epicenter of the Trump administration’s ramped-up immigration enforcement earlier this year. Two American citizens, Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti, were fatally shot by immigration officers in January amid protests in Minneapolis, fueling anger over the White House's hard-line approach to immigration and border security. Craig’s vote in support of the Laken Riley Act, which was passed in January 2025, has become a sticking point among many progressive voters. Craig has said she regrets voting for the bill. “It is true that the president is not using any laws to carry out these sweeping immigration raids that have terrorized Minnesotans, but it’s also become clear that supporting any bill that gives ICE new authority in this administration was the wrong decision. And I regret my vote,” she wrote in The Minneapolis Star-Tribune in March. Schultz said that Flanagan is “trying to make it about immigration and the Metro Surge, arguing that Craig was too weak in opposing Trump because she supported the Laken Riley Act.” “Those issues matter, but I think there are other dynamics at play that are being underappreciated. Turnout, money, organization, and the age profiles of the two candidates' supporters may prove just as important,” he said. Minnesota Is Latest Battle Between Progressives and Moderates Flanagan has received support from national progressive figures like Senator Bernie Sanders, a Vermont independent, Senator Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat and Representative Ilhan Omar, a Minnesota Democrat. Moderates such as former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg have backed Craig’s campaign. The race comes just one week after El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan, a key win for the left in a critical swing state. Progressives are hoping to pull off another victory in Minnesota on Tuesday. Schultz said that “on one level,” the race is a contest between the progressive and establishment wings of the Democratic Party. “However, Minnesota is not Michigan, and it is not New York City. Among the things we need to consider in this race is that Lieutenant Governor Flanagan has never won a statewide race on her own. She has won statewide as lieutenant governor as part of the Walz ticket,” he said. Therefore, Flanagan is “relatively untested,” and the state is more conservative outside of the Twin Cities area, he said. “That raises the question of whether she has sufficient appeal statewide, including within the Democratic Party, even though roughly 55 percent of the statewide vote comes from the Twin Cities metropolitan area,” he said. Sanders said on CBS News’ Face the Nation over the weekend that he is not confident in Flanagan’s chances, saying it is going to be a “tight race” and that he hopes “very much that Peggy wins.” “People are tired of status quo politics and establishment policies. They want real change and Peggy Flanagan is about bringing about real change, standing up to the big-money interests,” he said. “There is a reason why the super PACs and billionaires are flooding Minnesota with all kinds of money. The same thing as Michigan. They don’t want somebody to stand up for the working class in Minnesota.” What Do Prediction Markets Show? Prediction markets favored Flanagan as of Monday afternoon, with both Kalshi and Polymarket giving her a 72 percent chance of victory. Prediction markets allow traders to buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real‑money wagers into probability estimates. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment at a given moment but do not always accurately predict the future. Is Minnesota a Blue State? Republicans have targeted Minnesota in recent elections but have fallen short, as the state has retained its status as light blue. Minnesota last voted for a Republican at the presidential level in 1972 but has still given Democrats narrow margins in the latest presidential races. Harris carried the state by only about 4 points in 2024, a narrower win than former President Joe Biden’s 7-point victory in 2020. In 2016, Minnesota backed former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton by less than 2 percentage points. Former President Barack Obama did better in the state—carrying it by nearly 8 points in 2012 and more than 10 points in 2008. Minnesota last elected a Republican senator in 2002, backing Republican Norm Coleman. In 2008, he lost reelection to Democrat Al Franken. news.title: Trump should not save Hollywood with a tax credit — which wouldn’t even work
news.text:
President Donald Trump has no reason to reward a hostile Hollywood with federal tax credits — while leaving the industry’s underlying problems in California intact. 

The California Post reported over the weekend that former LA mayoral candidate Spencer Pratt recently met privately with President Donald Trump. His pitch: A 25% federal film-production tax credit to “bring back Hollywood.”

Pratt is not alone. Jon Voight, one of Trump’s special ambassadors to Hollywood, has promoted a federal production credit as part of a broader industry-revival plan. Sylvester Stallone has joined entertainment unions, studios and trade organizations urging the same.

They face a political problem before they ever reach the policy debate. Trump has a long memory, and Hollywood spent the past decade trying to keep him out of the Oval Office, then denouncing him once he got there anyway.

Robert De Niro called Trump “a punk,” “a dog,” “a pig” and “a con.” George Clooney branded him a “xenophobic fascist.” Tom Hanks dismissed him as a “simplistic, self-involved gasbag.”

Ron Howard described him as a “self-serving, dishonest, morally bankrupt ego maniac.” Arnold Schwarzenegger declared Trump would be remembered as the “worst president ever.” Harrison Ford recently said Trump “scares the s— out of me” and called him history’s greatest criminal.

Those are only a few examples. For years, the Oscars, Golden Globes, Emmys and SAG Awards doubled as venues for mocking Trump and lecturing his supporters. Anti-Trump politics became part of Hollywood’s institutional culture, not an occasional protest tied to one election.

The industry also put serious money behind Trump’s opponents in all three presidential campaigns.

In 2016, George Clooney hosted major fundraisers for Hillary Clinton, with Jeffrey Katzenberg, Steven Spielberg and Haim Saban among the co-hosts. The events generated an estimated $15 million.

In 2020, Clooney and Katzenberg raised $7 million for Joe Biden. A separate Saban event brought in $4.5 million more.

In 2024, Clooney, Julia Roberts, Barbra Streisand, Jimmy Kimmel and Katzenberg staged a gala that raised over $30 million for Biden. After the Democrats swapped in Kamala Harris, a fundraiser featuring Stevie Wonder, Jessica Alba and Lily Tomlin brought in another $28 million.

Hollywood remains entitled to equal treatment under the law. Its politics alone do not settle the tax-credit question. But the industry is asking a president it spent a decade attacking to approve a stand-alone federal subsidy, stacked on top of California’s own credits, for a business hardly starved for capital.

That is the politics. The policy case is the bigger problem, and it fails on its own terms.

Calling it a “tax credit” makes it sound less like spending. But if the credit is refundable and exceeds a company’s tax liability, Washington writes a check for the difference.

A 25% federal credit would stack atop state subsidies that already reach 35% to 40% in California. Taxpayers would cover expenses studios have always paid themselves. Backers will count entire production budgets as “economic impact,” although much of that work would happen anyway. Paying a company for something it already planned to do creates a windfall, not a job.

California’s nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office found no compelling evidence that the state’s film credit grows the economy after accounting for lost revenue and displaced activity.

The largest studios, with the deepest lobbying benches, will be best positioned to capture the benefit. Smaller producers will fight over whatever remains. Studios keep the profits when a production succeeds; taxpayers absorb part of the cost either way.

Download The California Post App, follow us on social, and subscribe to our newsletters 

Nor would the credit solve Hollywood’s larger problems: streaming upheaval, labor disruption and foreign competition. California has made the math worse through high taxes, costly energy and heavy statewide regulation, along with permitting headaches and public disorder in Los Angeles. Producers can read a spreadsheet. Sacramento’s answer is to pay favored companies to tolerate costs it should lower for everyone.

A federal credit would leave California’s competitiveness problem intact while making the rest of the country underwrite it. Lower taxes and lighter regulation for every business would do more than another carveout for a connected industry.

Hollywood had every right to campaign against Trump. But it used its cultural reach and financial machinery against him in three straight campaigns, mocking him from awards stages, insulting him in interviews and raising tens of millions for Clinton, Biden and Harris. Now it wants his signature on a subsidy of its own, making the current ask a harder sell than its backers seem to appreciate.

The federal tax code already contains too many special provisions secured by industries with powerful lobbying operations. A private meeting and a glossy economic-impact projection are not reasons to add another.

The answer should be simple: No federal Hollywood tax credit. Let Hollywood compete, and let California fix what California broke.

Jon Fleischman, a longtime strategist in California politics, writes at SoDoesItMatter.com.

news.title: Tuesday’s primaries will give Democrats a big idea on how much the left has taken hold of the party
news.text:
Michigan’s primary is over, but another pair of tests loom for the progressive left.

On Tuesday, voters in two midwestern states will decide a pair of races that have become the latest battlegrounds of the Democratic Party’s ongoing civil war. In Wisconsin, progressive candidate Francesca Hong is leading in all available polling in the Democratic primary for governor. 

In Minnesota, a much tighter race is depicted in polling between Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan and Rep. Angie Craig in another highly-watched Senate race, which comes just a week after the victory of progressive populist Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan.

Craig, like El-Sayed’s opponent Haley Stevens, is backed by centrist Democratic Party leadership figures such as Hakeem Jeffries, Nancy Pelosi and Elissa Slotkin. Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer hasn’t publicly put a thumb on the scale, and Democratic senators are urging him and the party’s campaign arm to stay out of it — largely due to their toxic brand. Flanagan, backed by Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren as well as the retiring incumbent, Tina Smith, narrowly trailed Craig in a recent SurveyUSA poll that showed nearly one in five voters still undecided. 

Hong, a true political outsider, lacks the kind of national support as Flanagan but is backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, the far-left group which continues to grow bolder with the successive primary victories of left-leaning candidates this cycle. Members of the group formed part of the volunteer army that helped El-Sayed push past a mountain of outside PAC spending to victory in the Michigan primary, though El-Sayed himself is not a member. As a former chef, Hong has leaned on her working class background as she runs an insurgent campaign defying the party's elites.

A victory in one or both races tomorrow will be another rallying cry for the left.

Hong’s momentum is due in large part to her early, energetic campaign style and breakout messaging that established her as a frontrunner early and fractured her opposition. 

Her opponents and the party’s centrist wing remained divided, unwilling to fully coalesce behind her closest rival, Mandela Barnes, for months. Barnes then withdrew, leaving Milwaukee County executive David Crowley on deck to jump in and try to stop Hong’s momentum.

Should she win a commanding victory Tuesday, many on the left will quickly wipe the bad taste from their mouth that lingered after El-Sayed’s margin of victory in Michigan was far, far closer than expected.

If Craig also loses, it will be a sign of not just the organization of the far left, which remains a powerful theme of the 2026 cycle. It will also signal a deep anger that seems to exist among the Democratic Party’s electorate nationwide, not just in far-left neighborhoods of New York City where party leaders initially hoped to contain the DSA and the anti-establishment fury. 

The 2024 defeat of Kamala Harris left many Democrats nationwide feeling angry and hopeless, and furious at a party elite that denied voters a primary, then selected a nominee after it was clear that the president, Joe Biden, could no longer run.

Action in 2025 only poured gasoline on that fire as repeated calls for Democrats to withhold votes on key legislation and prevent the Trump administration from operating in a business-as-usual atmosphere seemed to fall on deaf ears at times, even as Elon Musk’s DOGE staffers began taking a hammer to the federal government.

On the other hand, a victory by Craig would be a significant message to party leadership, too. The congresswoman is one of her party’s true moderates, having voted for the Laken Riley Act last year and being known for working across the aisle with Republicans on other issues. She, like Stevens in Michigan, has also been supported by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee in the past — though the race differs significantly from Michigan in that the pro-Israel lobby has not spent tens of millions of dollars to protect one candidate.

Flanagan, while not aligned with DSA, is much closer in attitude to the far-left group: “Whatever word you want to use, [ICE] can’t exist like this anymore,” she told the New York Times of her own views of immigration enforcement. “We have to rip ICE apart and start over.”

Should Craig manage to pull it off a win on Tuesday, her victory would symbolize the enduring appetite of Democratic voters for a stricter law enforcement attitude, even as most find the mass deportation strategy deplorable and opposed the “surge” of enforcement in Minneapolis that ended with federal agents withdrawing partially after the deaths of two protesters in confrontations with ICE and immigration enforcement authorities.

Democrats could wake up Wednesday morning to the creation of a powerful midwestern bloc of progressive candidates having sprung up before their eyes. Counting El-Sayed and Will Lawrence in Michigan (who won his primary despite AIPAC-related groups highlighting his old criticism of Black political leaders), four victories by progressives in high-profile races within two weeks will leave many in the Beltway feeling anxious about the scope of the transformation the party is currently undergoing.
news.summary: Michigan’s primary is over. The left’s takeover of the Midwest may have just begun, and that’s bad news for an establishment that thought it could contain them, writes John Bowden

news.title: Abdul El-Sayed turns toward Michigan’s general election after a bruising primary
news.text:
It is the first full week of Abdul El-Sayed’s run for the Senate, and there is no rest. Shaking off the exhaustion he acknowledged at the end of a grueling primary campaign and wearing a suit and tie instead of his usual black V-neck T-shirt, he made his first stop on two Sunday morning TV appearances. 

He found himself answering questions emerging from the right about his “radical” politics that some paint as “dangerous,” which gave the new Democratic nominee an opportunity to workshop a response.

“They’re going to try and paint me as a certain thing, given my name. But I also think it’s important for us to recognize that America has a long history of embracing,” El-Sayed said on NBC’s “Meet the Press.” “America is a lot bigger than very small people like Donald Trump or JD Vance or Mike Rogers want to make it out to be.” 

Attempting to turn these questions back on his foes will need to be part of the Democrat’s general election campaign, after his win in last week’s divisive Michigan Democratic primary for U.S. Senate made him a face of the resurgence of progressive politics. His campaign is now working at hyperspeed to organize all the demands that come with victory — interviews, events, social media and meetings with voters. 

El-Sayed overcame a gigantic financial disadvantage in his primary against Rep. Haley Stevens, and he may have to deal with the same cash disparity against the GOP nominee, former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers, in November given that the Midwestern state may be the GOP’s best chance to flip a Senate seat as it seeks to hold on to its majority in that chamber. 

At the same time, keeping the Michigan seat is critical to Democrats’ hopes of winning control of the Senate. 

Given the stakes and the fierceness of party politics in the Trump era, the challenge for El-Sayed is to bring his own party together while getting ready to answer what is expected to be an onslaught from the right.

“As divisive and as cynical as the campaign against us might have been, I want us to realize that there is so much more that unites us now,” El-Sayed said at a recent event. “Because the campaign that Mike Rogers and Donald Trump and their GOP MAGA allies are launching is already more bitter.” 

“As divisive and as cynical as the campaign against us might have been, I want us to realize that there is so much more that unites us now.”Michigan Senate nominee Abdul-El-Sayedmi

Republicans are already pitching the argument they will use against him. 

“El-Sayed is not just another Democrat; he’s the most radical Senate nominee in U.S. history,” the Senate GOP’s campaign arm said in a recent memo in which they pointed out, without nuance, some of the positions he has taken in the past and the difficulty of what he is trying to accomplish. “The Democrat primary results show their party is deeply divided with nearly half of voters rejecting El-Sayed. Nothing indicates he will be able to unite his party or build a working class coalition, but Michigan is a true 50/50 battleground where we cannot take a single vote for granted,” the memo stated. 

Former Democratic Rep. Dan Kildee, who won six terms in Michigan before retiring in 2024, acknowledged the challenges that come with the GOP portraying El-Sayed as extreme. 

“Friends of mine outside of Michigan who are more moderate Democrats are in full panic mode,” Kildee said. “I tell them El-Sayed has to fight to be defined around his populist message and not the identity politics. And voters ultimately do want their interests to be central to this debate. So no matter what the question is, the answer has to be about the chaos Donald Trump brings and what it means to your paycheck.”

El-Sayed’s message for the moment reflects that. While many Democrats talk about affordability, he has distilled that issue into a mantra his supporters chant at rallies: Money out of politics. Money in your pocket. Medicare for all. 

On “Meet the Press,” El-Sayed also described a phone call with former President Barack Obama, the fellow Democrat who knows what it is to enter a campaign as an underdog. Their talk, El-Sayed said, was “really warm,” with Obama offering advice. The former president won Michigan both times he ran and is Democrats’ most sought-after surrogate. Asked if Obama would campaign for him, El-Sayed answered on the show, “I really hope so.”

The campaign confirms that there have also been calls with other top Democrats who, not coincidentally, are also 2028 presidential hopefuls, including California Gov. Gavin Newsom, Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly and Maryland Gov. Wes Moore. 

The quick moves to rally around El-Sayed after the close primary could be because of the message a frustrated electorate sent through his primary victory. Or it could be that his personal political ambitions are tied to the broader ambitions of the party, and what Democrats’ success or failure in the key battleground will mean come presidential election season. 

Another 2028 hopeful, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, spoke Friday night in Detroit, calling the nasty and divisive Senate primary “spirited.” It was positive spin at a rally meant to bring a fractured party together, with supporters waving hopeful signs reading “One Team Michigan.”

Buttigieg was far from the only Michigander taking the mic. 

So did Mallory McMorrow, who, in spite of dropping out 30 days before the primary, won 4%, or 61,407 votes, in a race decided by fewer than 16,000 votes. She is already stumping for El-Sayed, and Stevens has said she will too. His campaign quickly put out a press release saying he brought in $2.3 million in the 48 hours after he clinched the nomination, a nice bump for a campaign that refuses all corporate donations. 

The euphoria of the nominee’s supporters comes with major reality checks. There are two key voting blocs he lost in the primary: the Black vote and the Jewish vote.

His team hopes the endorsement of former Vice President Kamala Harris and support from Obama will help with Black voters. In the wave of meetings he plans to take are some with Jewish leaders concerned about both his policy positions and his rhetoric, though El-Sayed has repeatedly denounced antisemitism. 

A lot can happen in 85 days; the world is volatile and voters can be fickle. But Kildee sees an opening. “What I hear from folks here is the people that Trump has lost haven’t fallen out of love with him, they just don’t see him serving their best interests any longer,” he said.

He added, of El-Sayed’s win, “I’m not sure I’d go so far as to say it’s a defining moment [for the party] but it is a moment when Democrats want candidates to stand for something, be about something, not just anti-Trump. You have to convince them what you can do.”

Hunter Woodall contributed to this report.

news.title: AOC Speaks Out Against Woke, Sparks Left-Wing Backlash
news.text: Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a New York Democrat who many progressives hope will run for president in 2028, has faced a wave of left-wing backlash over comments at the weekend which have been interpreted as her speaking out against woke. Ocasio-Cortez was asked during an interview on ABC News’ This Week on Sunday about remarks made by Wisconsin governor candidate Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist whose old social media posts about Thanksgiving have become a sticking point ahead of her primary on Tuesday. In 2020, Hong said on Twitter: "Cancel Thanksgiving. Should have done this in 1621." She has since backtracked from that, saying recently: "I'm not going to cancel Thanksgiving," and "I will be celebrating Thanksgiving with my family this year." Congresswoman Ocasio-Cortez was pressed by this This Week host Jonathan Karl for her thoughts about Hong's past position, and her reactions highlight the shift by many progressives away from "woke" culture and policies such as defunding the police embraced by many on the left around 2020. "My understanding is that Francesca Hong has made clear her present stances to her electorate," she said. She agreed with the host that Hong had now rowed back from her Thanksgiving remark. "She’s moved away from it. I have a local city councilman that has this saying, ‘Woke 1 was crazy.’ I think that what’s important is that we have to assess what a candidate is saying now." She viewed the culture amid the COVID-19 pandemic as a "huge opening of the Overton window." "The doors were really open in trying to entertain any and every policy that was going to get us to a better place," she said. "I actually think that the discussions that we had in that time were quite fruitful. I think that when we talk about crime today, it’s fundamentally different than the way that we talked about crime and bringing crime down." Newsweek reached out to Ocasio-Cortez’s team for comment via email. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez ‘Woke 1’ Remarks Draw Left-Wing Backlash Ocasio-Cortez’s comments were taken as 'speaking out against woke' by some on the left, sparking criticism. Briahna Joy Gray, a progressive commentator who served as Senator Bernie Sanders' 2020 presidential campaign press secretary, wrote in response to Ocasio-Cortez in a post on X, "LOLZ George Floyd was crazy! I was like, Black lives? Jkjkjk." Kate Willett, a comedian and writer, also took issue with Ocasio-Cortez’s remarks. "I know that most members of National DSA anticipate riding her coattails would boost our numbers but not if she’s denouncing DSA and socialism the whole time lol. I know I’m in the minority but I see no advantage to debasing ourselves for this," she wrote on X. Journalist Alex Colston wrote that people describe the era as if it was "reducible to chaotic intra-elite discourse and panic," but that it only occurred due to "the largest uprising in U.S. history that same year." "The ruling class did not handle that very well, who would deny? They freaked out, and cycled through every known trope of liberal political correctness and deference, but somehow they never addressed the reason for the uprising in the first place: police murdering people," he wrote. The progressive account @ProudSocialist, which has more than 400,000 followers on X, said "Woke 1” was "not crazy." "What is crazy is U.S. cities have police budgets that are bigger than the military budgets of entire countries. Reallocating police funding to healthcare and housing is a common-sense solution rooted in justice," the account wrote. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez Chances of Winning 2028 Primary Ocasio-Cortez has been named as a potential 2028 presidential candidate who could consolidate support among the party’s left-leaning flank—particularly as several recent primaries suggest there is more of an appetite among the party’s primary electorate for a more left-leaning candidate. Her endorsed candidate Abdul El-Sayed defeated Representative Haley Stevens in Michigan’s Senate primary earlier in August, delivering a political victory to Ocasio-Cortez. Ocasio-Cortez said on This Week she is focused on Democrats winning the midterms but that she hasn’t "ruled out the possibility" of running for president. "I’m very humbled for the tremendous amount of support out there," she said. "I think that we have a responsibility to remain focused on the midterms and not on our individual aspirations or plans." She has also been floated as a potential candidate to run against Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, a New York Democrat who has faced criticism from the base over what many Democrats view as a feeble response to Trump’s administration. The latest polls, however, show other more moderate candidates with an early lead. Early polling this far out is not necessarily definitive but can be a key signal to fundraisers about a candidate’s name recognition and popularity. As the primary begins and candidates begin making their cases to voters, polling can always shift. An Emerson College poll, which surveyed 574 likely voters from July 19-20, showed Ocasio-Cortez received 13 percent of the vote, behind former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg (19 percent) and California Governor Gavin Newsom (17 percent). Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff also received 13 percent, while former Vice President Kamala Harris polled at 8 percent. A McLaughlin & Associates poll showed Harris in the lead (28 percent), followed by Newsom (17 percent), Ocasio-Cortez (10 percent) and Buttigieg (8 percent). It surveyed 472 likely voters from July 15-21. Ocasio-Cortez is among the top candidates in prediction markets as well. As of Monday, Kalshi showed Newsom having the greatest chance of winning the Democratic primary with 16 percent, followed by both Ocasio-Cortez and Ossoff at 15 percent. On Polymarket, Newsom led with 18 percent, followed by Ossoff at 16 percent and Ocasio-Cortez at 15 percent.
