news.title: La Gaceta Full Endorsements
news.text:
U.S. Senate

Alex Vindman gets our endorsement over Angie Nixon.
Nixon is a state representative, union organizer, well qualified and offers to fight for lower costs, higher wages and to wrestle control of our government out of the hands of the uber rich and give it back to the people.
Vindman offers much of the same as Nixon, but Vindman has a better chance at defeating U.S. Senator Ashley Moody.
Lieutenant Colonel Vindman gained a national following when in 2019 he reported on and testified about a phone call between President Donald Trump and the Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy when Trump pressured for the Ukrainians to investigate Joe Biden in exchange for U.S. military assistance.
That fame led to a huge amount of small-dollar donations nationally. It will take money to unseat Moody. Vindman is qualified, has experience in foreign affairs and national security, and wants to get government working for us and not Trump Inc and his fellow robber barons.

Congress, District 12

We like both of these candidates. Kimberly Overman is a former county commissioner and a certified financial planner who fought hard for affordable housing and expanded healthcare access. She fought against human trafficking and special interests manipulating government.
Darren McAuley is a doctor, a Colonel in the Air National Guard, served as State Air Surgeon for Florida and is the leading expert on osteopathic practices at the Orlando College of Osteopathic Medicine. He’s been in the military for 25 years and served in six deployments. He’s mad about the gutting of Medicaid and cutting healthcare to thousands here in Florida, the weakening of FEMA, the attacks on voting rights, and tariffs, which are fueling inflation and are a tax on working families.
McAuley has been a stronger fundraiser and his military service will help him wrestle veterans away from voting for the incumbent, Republican Congressman Gus Bilirakis.
We endorse McAuley, believing he has a better chance of winning the general election.
District 15

Two military men, Christopher Irizarry and Robert People, are vying for a chance to challenge Republican Congresswoman Laurel Lee. People joined the Army at 18 and served 21 years, having two combat tours in Iraq and one in Afghanistan. He retired in 2018.
Irizarry served eight years in the Army and 16 years in the CIA. Both candidates are supporters of expanding healthcare, stronger public schools, unions, protecting our environment and reducing runaway costs of everything.
We endorse both candidates. The winner doesn’t really have a chance against Congresswoman Lee, as the district has been redrawn to make it almost impossible for a Democrat to win.

U.S. Senate and Congress District 14-Republican
All the major candidates will echo whatever Trump says. They will let him steal power away from the legislative and judicial branches. They will turn their heads while he and his hench men steal tax dollars.
We can’t endorse any of them.

There are six candidates, but only one has a chance to bring the fight to the likely Republican nominee Byron Donalds.
That person is David Jolly and his running mate for lieutenant governor, Gwen Graham, and we wholeheartedly endorse the team.
Jolly is smart, even tempered, middle of the road and understands how government should work. Graham has the same qualities, and both served in Congress.
Our current governor sold us out to big insurance. Jolly wants to restore the balance by creating a catastrophic fund to reduce costs and make insurance pay their claims. He wants to help condominium associations with no-interest, state-backed loans so they can fix old buildings that suffer from years of neglected maintenance.
He wants to rein in school vouchers and invest in public schools. Under Jolly, climate change will be addressed in policies from resiliency to energy to transportation. He also wants to end the culture war which seems to occupy most of our state government’s time and energy.

The Republicans are favoring their DEI candidate Byron Donalds. He’s their minority and a complete Trump devotee. We think he’s completely unqualified. We endorse Donalds, believing he’ll be an easier target for Democrat David Jolly.

Chief Financial Officer

Earle Ford is an army airborne infantry veteran, a former assistant state attorney and a federal investigator for the Internal Revenue Service. His background fits the job and he wants to provide spending oversight, government accountability and property insurance reform.
Annette Tadeo has served in the Florida State Senate, ran a small business and unsuccessfully ran for lieutenant governor as Charlie Crist’s running mate. She was born in Colombia. She also wants to reduce property insurance costs and be an independent watchdog of taxpayer dollars. We haven’t had a watchdog in that office for quite some time, which is why we wasted millions on Alligator Alcatraz, saw the governor steal Medicaid money to fund political campaigns and overpay for beach property, and give away state lands.
We will support Earle Ford, as he has a better resume for the job.

Blaise Ingoglia is the incumbent, having been appointed by Governor Ronald DeSantis. He has ignored his responsibility of being a watchdog of tax dollars. He has refused to look into the huge amount of waste caused by the governor – Alligator Alcatraz, spending on the governor’s personal state guard, no-bid contracts, land giveaways and the theft of Medicaid dollars for non-political campaigns.
We endorse Frank W. Collige. He is a business owner, served in the Air Force, has a great beard and promises financial transparency and accountability. Ingoglia promises to be the next governor’s puppet, and not the good kind with strings.

Commissioner of Agriculture

Joey Mendoza Atkins and Donald A. “Don” Prichard are competing in hopes of taking on incumbent Wilton Simpson, who is most likely to win the Republican primary.
Neither Mendoza Atkins nor Prichard seemed to be running much of a campaign. Mendoza Atkins is an attorney, a former sports agent and is currently with the Barnes Trial Group in Miami.
Prichard is a captain with the Pembroke Park Police Department in South Florida. He previously served with the Broward County Sheriff’s Office for 24 years. He also served with the Florida Army National Guard. We can’t find enough information on either one to make an endorsement. Neither one seems to be campaigning. Either one would face a tough battle in trying to defeat Simpson.

Matt Taylor is challenging Wilton Simpson, the incumbent.
Taylor goes by “Matt the Welder” and is a somewhat comical political figure. At one time, he posted nude photos of himself on the web and got mad that the issue has come up now that he’s running for office. He said it wasn’t porn because he wasn’t paid.
Our choice is Wilton Simpson. He is the class act on the top of the Republican ticket for cabinet. He understands agriculture, having been in the egg business. He is reasonable and has a soft spot in his heart for foster children. We are disappointed in his votes on the cabinet. He voted in solidarity with the governor on some bad deals. We hope he is a more independent voice on the cabinet in the future.

State Senate
District 16
Universal primary
This race pits State Representative Fentrice Driskell against State Representative Michele Rayner. Both are Democrats
Rayner was first elected as state representative in 2020. She is an attorney focused on civil rights and promotes that she was the first openly queer Black member of the Florida Legislature. She has attracted progressive elements of the party to support her.
Driskell won her first race for state representative in 2018. She is also an attorney who works for Carlton Fields in business litigation. She attended Harvard University and finished law school at Georgetown University.
Driskell and Rayner are native Floridians. Driskell made history as the first Black woman elected as House Democratic Leader. She has lots of support from current and former Democratic officials.
The public can’t go wrong with either candidate but we will endorse Fentrice Driskell. 
Democrats hold a minority position in the House and Senate and are mostly on the sidelines of governing. We expect the few Democrats in the Legislature to focus on improving the Democrat brand with voters and organizing elected Democrats to speak with a more unified voice. They need a more populous agenda to try to box in Republicans and show the true nature of the many harmful bills that pass both chambers.
Rayner had a very safe seat while Driskell had to win a State House seat that was competitive. We believe having to appeal to independent voters as Driskell did was better training for the difficult job ahead of helping position Democrats to win more seats and improve the party’s approval with voters.

State Representative
District 62
Universal primary
Both candidates are Democrats
Wengay “Newt” Newton has experience as a state representative and a St. Petersburg city councilman. He prides himself on being able to reach across the aisle to bring home some wins for his district in a Republican-dominated house.
Kyandra Darling worked for Democratic Congressman Charlie Crist and later as an aide to St. Petersburg council members Steve Kornell and Lisa Wheeler-Bowman. She worked for nonprofits and helped with Kamala Harris’ campaign in the Bay Area. Darling wants to focus on affordability, access to healthcare and addiction treatment. We find her a great addition to the Democratic bench and with the skill set will help expand the party’s appeal to independents.
We endorse Kyandra Darling for State House.
District 63
Universal primary
All three candidates are Democrats
Jacqueline Coffie-Leeks is the executive director of Sulphur Springs Neighborhood of Promise Initiative and Pastor of Outreach at 34th Street Church of God. She is heavily involved in the community and an advocate for the poor and underserved.
Robin Lockett is also an advocate and community leader and is the Regional Director of Florida Rising Tampa Bay. She knows the district and has fought for affordable housing.
Conrad Schupay’s family settled here after his father retired from the Air Force. He attended local schools in the district and eventually was accepted to and graduated West Point. He served in the military for 24 years in the Army and Florida Army National Guard and had two deployments to Afghanistan.
He worked for the City of Tampa and the financial industry.
We like all three candidates. They are supportive of increasing healthcare access, affordability and focusing Florida’s government on what working people need and not the culture war currently being fought. We endorse all three, as we believe any one of them would be a fine addition to the State Legislature.
District 64

We did not interview any of the candidates in this race, as we know each and are familiar with their histories.
John Rodriguez knows the legislative process and could start to be productive on day one. He served as aide to several state legislators who served the district. He worked in St. Petersburg city government for mayor Rick Kriseman. He now works at the property appraiser’s office. We find Rodriguez to be knowledgeable and passionate about public service.
Mike Suarez served on City council. He has roots here and knows the district. We were unhappy with some of Suarez’ City Council votes and found him to be uninterested in opposing views. We are also concerned that his largest donor is the insurance industry.
Luis Salazar is our pick. He is young, energetic and has the most passion for serving in Tallahassee. He is a great addition to the Democratic slate and has helped get other Democrats elected with grassroots work. Salazar served in the Navy. He is a community activist and a social media marketer. He listens, learns fast and can help build the Democratic Party. His agenda is to rein in big insurance, utilities and expand affordable housing. He is bilingual, which is also a plus.

There are three names on the ballot, Amaro Lionheart, Angel Ramos and Dan Weldon. Lionheart has withdrawn from the race, so a vote for him will not count.
Angel Ramos was born in Puerto Rico and made the move to Tampa much later in life. He’s had a varied work history, ranging from programmer, marketing strategist, entertainment and private investigation. His positions show that he wants to protect students from indoctrination at public schools that is not happening. He supports removing vaccine mandates for children.
Dan Weldon is a former prosecutor and currently a litigation lawyer. He played for the UF football team and was statewide chair of the College Republicans of Florida.
He wrote to the Tampa Bay Times, “The cost of having and raising children is at an all-time high. Job opportunities for young people are some of the worst they’ve ever been … our future is being left behind.”
It’s a pretty bleak viewpoint for a conservative activist considering his party controls the Federal and State governments. Trump says, under his regime, that America is great – it’s thriving.
We endorse Weldon in this race. He seems to be more informed and probably less conservative than he thinks he is.

County Commission

Incumbent County Commissioner Gwen Myers is being challenged by Twanda Bradley. Bradley retired from the IT industry after 30 years and is focused on property investment and management. She also has a nonprofit which provides food and supports the community. She is pleasant, positive and listens.
Myers is become an effective commissioner for her district since 2020 and is a strong advocate for the district’s needs. Myers is independent of special interests and is also involved in the community. Her background is in county government. She knows the system and delivers county investment in poor and underserved areas of our county.
We endorse Gwen Myers for re-election to the Commission

Stacy Hahn is a School Board member trying to graduate to County Commission. She’s never impressed us on the School Board. She refused to hold the superintendent and other top staffers accountable for accepting a gift, a trip to Augusta National , from a vendor. She is pushing for tax cuts but has accepted in her PAC a $5,000 contribution from Ken Babby so she is happy to write a big tax dollar check to the Tampa Bay Rays. While on the School Board, she was paid to lure public school students to go to charter and private schools, which undermines our public schools.
Incumbent County Commissioner Donna Cameron Cepeda opposed the Rays deal, especially using CIT dollars, which is a plus in our eyes.
She is for using limited tax dollars to improve roads and other critical infrastructure. She is consistent in that voting.
We endorse Cepeda in the Republican primary.

Democrats have two good choices, Aileen Rodriguez and Cindy Stuart. Stuart has a lot of experience governing. She was a School Board member for eight years and then ran to replace the retiring Pat Frank for Clerk of the Circuit Court. She won that seat. After one term, she was defeated by Republican Victor Crist. Stuart knows how the county works and can be productive starting on day one.
Rodriguez was born in Puerto Rico and raised in Hillsborough County on a dairy farm. She got her first taste of politics as a regional director for U.S. Senator Mel Martinez. She stopped being a registered Republican in 2019 because that party did not reflect her values. She has her own public relations company and has worked for a wide range of well-known companies, governments and nonprofits in the area.
She is excited about public service, a good listener and a quick learner.
In talking to both about the potential Rays deal, both leaned to supporting it, but Rodriguez was interested in learning more, both pro and con.
It’s a close call but we will endorse Aileen Rodriguez for her enthusiasm and willingness to hear both sides of an issue.

School Board
District 2 – Nonpartisan
This district covers South Tampa and parts of East Hillsborough County. Brittany Lyssy is a young mother, an attorney and the former chair of the Hillsborough County Young Republicans. She is sharp, presents well, but in the past, she supported vouchers and charter schools. We want a School Board member focused on making public schools great, not expanding alternatives to public schools.
Chris Taylor was a teacher and converted over to owning and running businesses and is now executive vice president of a company that mines Bitcoin, validates blockchain transactions and hosts mining software. He’s also chair of the Hillsborough Education Foundation. He is smart and has experience in schools and business, which would be good for the School Board. He is also dismissive of his female opponents. That won’t work well on a board full of women.
Daniela Simic is our pick. She has a long resume in education. She knows the district’s strengths and more importantly, its weaknesses. She also worked in other districts and in private business, which helps her to bring in new and different ideas. She has the skills to work well with fellow board members and she has the confidence of the teachers’ union. She also has a child in a local public school. She is passionate about education, a good listener and smart.
District 6 – Nonpartisan
Incumbent Karen Perez is being challenged by Kenneth “Ken” Gay and Sally Harris “Ms Sally” Williamson. While the race is nonpartisan, party affiliation sometimes provides more clarity. Perez is a Democrat being challenged by two Republicans.
Gay has been a teacher for close to four decades and is now retired. He ran for School Board before. He sees one of the challenges is creating an environment where teachers can enjoy their job, feel safe and feel appreciated. Low pay isn’t the only reason people are leaving the profession.
Harris Williamson served on the School Board from 2014 to 2018. She is a long-time preschool owner in South Tampa. She has run a couple of times unsuccessfully. She now lives in Plant City. Harris knows the school district, works well with others and is passionate about children.
We endorse Karen Perez. She is a strong advocate for underserved children in the district. She is fiscally responsible. As a clinical social worker, she knows the importance of addressing mental health issues of students. She was first elected in 2018 and provides a unique perspective on the Board.

Circuit Judge
13th Judicial Circuit

This race has two qualified candidates who are personable. Luis “Louie” Aguila is a native. His family owned the La Ideal Sandwich Shop in West Tampa. He was assistant state attorney under Mark Ober, Andrew Warren and Suzy Lopez. He is now with the statewide prosecutor’s office and handles cases in several counties. He has over a decade of legal experience.
Our pick is Sara Peacock. Peacock has 15 years of legal experience in criminal defense, family law and civil litigation. Her mother has been a judge for years, so she knows what the job entails. She is involved in her community, the Bar and in improving the legal profession. We think she’ll make a great judge.

The public can’t go wrong in this race where Nina McGucken Alvarez and Jim Wimsatt are vying for votes.
McGucken Alvarez has 17 years of experience in the areas of family law, probate, guardianship. She is assistant regional counsel and represents indigent clients with developmental disabilities. She’s been a sole practitioner much of her career. She is a third-generation Tampeña. She operates with honesty and integrity.
Jim Wimsatt has practiced for 22 years, focused on family law. He is with Harris Hunt & Derr PA. He is rated AV Preeminent by Martindale-Hubbell. His community service involves Metropolitan Ministries, Trinity Cafe and the Community Food Pantry. He is a Georgetown University Law Center graduate. Wimsatt is passionate about the law and fair.
It’s a close call. We will endorse Wimsatt, who has more years of experience and a history of community service.

news.title: Abdul El-Sayed’s turn towards Michigan’s general election
news.text:
It is the first full week of Abdul El-Sayed’s run for the Senate, and there is no rest. Shaking off the exhaustion he acknowledged at the end of a grueling primary campaign and wearing a suit and tie instead of his usual black V-neck T-shirt, he made his first stop on two Sunday morning TV appearances. 

He found himself answering questions emerging from the right about his “radical” politics that some paint as “dangerous,” which gave the new Democratic nominee an opportunity to workshop a response.

“They’re going to try and paint me as a certain thing, given my name. But I also think it’s important for us to recognize that America has a long history of embracing,” El-Sayed said on NBC’s “Meet the Press.” “America is a lot bigger than very small people like Donald Trump or JD Vance or Mike Rogers want to make it out to be.” 

Attempting to turn these questions back on his foes will need to be part of the Democrat’s general election campaign, after his win in last week’s divisive Michigan Democratic primary for U.S. Senate made him a face of the resurgence of progressive politics. His campaign is now working at hyperspeed to organize all the demands that come with victory — interviews, events, social media and meetings with voters. 

El-Sayed overcame a gigantic financial disadvantage in his primary against Rep. Haley Stevens, and he may have to deal with the same cash disparity against the GOP nominee, former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers, in November given that the Midwestern state may be the GOP’s best chance to flip a Senate seat as it seeks to hold on to its majority in that chamber. 

At the same time, keeping the Michigan seat is critical to Democrats’ hopes of winning control of the Senate. 

Given the stakes and the fierceness of party politics in the Trump era, the challenge for El-Sayed is to bring his own party together while getting ready to answer what is expected to be an onslaught from the right.

“As divisive and as cynical as the campaign against us might have been, I want us to realize that there is so much more that unites us now,” El-Sayed said at a recent event. “Because the campaign that Mike Rogers and Donald Trump and their GOP MAGA allies are launching is already more bitter.” 

“As divisive and as cynical as the campaign against us might have been, I want us to realize that there is so much more that unites us now.”Michigan Senate nominee Abdul-El-Sayedmi

Republicans are already pitching the argument they will use against him. 

“El-Sayed is not just another Democrat; he’s the most radical Senate nominee in U.S. history,” the Senate GOP’s campaign arm said in a recent memo in which they pointed out, without nuance, some of the positions he has taken in the past and the difficulty of what he is trying to accomplish. “The Democrat primary results show their party is deeply divided with nearly half of voters rejecting El-Sayed. Nothing indicates he will be able to unite his party or build a working class coalition, but Michigan is a true 50/50 battleground where we cannot take a single vote for granted,” the memo stated. 

Former Democratic Rep. Dan Kildee, who won six terms in Michigan before retiring in 2024, acknowledged the challenges that come with the GOP portraying El-Sayed as extreme. 

“Friends of mine outside of Michigan who are more moderate Democrats are in full panic mode,” Kildee said. “I tell them El-Sayed has to fight to be defined around his populist message and not the identity politics. And voters ultimately do want their interests to be central to this debate. So no matter what the question is, the answer has to be about the chaos Donald Trump brings and what it means to your paycheck.”

El-Sayed’s message for the moment reflects that. While many Democrats talk about affordability, he has distilled that issue into a mantra his supporters chant at rallies: Money out of politics. Money in your pocket. Medicare for all. 

On “Meet the Press,” El-Sayed also described a phone call with former President Barack Obama, the fellow Democrat who knows what it is to enter a campaign as an underdog. Their talk, El-Sayed said, was “really warm,” with Obama offering advice. The former president won Michigan both times he ran and is Democrats’ most sought-after surrogate. Asked if Obama would campaign for him, El-Sayed answered on the show, “I really hope so.”

The campaign confirms that there have also been calls with other top Democrats who, not coincidentally, are also 2028 presidential hopefuls, including California Gov. Gavin Newsom, Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly and Maryland Gov. Wes Moore. 

The quick moves to rally around El-Sayed after the close primary could be because of the message a frustrated electorate sent through his primary victory. Or it could be that his personal political ambitions are tied to the broader ambitions of the party, and what Democrats’ success or failure in the key battleground will mean come presidential election season. 

Another 2028 hopeful, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, spoke Friday night in Detroit, calling the nasty and divisive Senate primary “spirited.” It was positive spin at a rally meant to bring a fractured party together, with supporters waving hopeful signs reading “One Team Michigan.”

Buttigieg was far from the only Michigander taking the mic. 

So did Mallory McMorrow, who, in spite of dropping out 30 days before the primary, won 4%, or 61,407 votes, in a race decided by fewer than 16,000 votes. She is already stumping for El-Sayed, and Stevens has said she will too. His campaign quickly put out a press release saying he brought in $2.3 million in the 48 hours after he clinched the nomination, a nice bump for a campaign that refuses all corporate donations. 

The euphoria of the nominee’s supporters comes with major reality checks. There are two key voting blocs he lost in the primary: the Black vote and the Jewish vote.

His team hopes the endorsement of former Vice President Kamala Harris and support from Obama will help with Black voters. In the wave of meetings he plans to take are some with Jewish leaders concerned about both his policy positions and his rhetoric, though El-Sayed has repeatedly denounced antisemitism. 

A lot can happen in 85 days; the world is volatile and voters can be fickle. But Kildee sees an opening. “What I hear from folks here is the people that Trump has lost haven’t fallen out of love with him, they just don’t see him serving their best interests any longer,” he said.

He added, of El-Sayed’s win, “I’m not sure I’d go so far as to say it’s a defining moment [for the party] but it is a moment when Democrats want candidates to stand for something, be about something, not just anti-Trump. You have to convince them what you can do.”

Hunter Woodall contributed to this report.

news.title: Pete Buttigieg to headline major South Carolina Democrats conference
news.text:
Early polling suggests Buttigieg would be among the leading contenders if he enters the race. A poll of likely 2028 Democratic primary voters in New Hampshire conducted last month found Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) leading the field with 22% support, followed closely by Buttigieg at 21%.

Sen. Mark Kelly (D-AZ) received 9%, Gov. Gavin Newsom (D-CA) received 8%, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) received 6%, and former Vice President Kamala Harris received 5%.

The poll offers an early glimpse at a contest in which no candidate has formally launched a campaign. It also comes more than 17 months before the first expected Democratic presidential primary in South Carolina.

The Democratic National Committee’s Rules and Bylaws Committee voted recently to make South Carolina the first state to hold a 2028 presidential primary.

Under the proposed calendar, South Carolina’s primary would be held Jan. 22, 2028, followed by Nevada on Feb. 1, New Hampshire on Feb. 8, New Mexico on Feb. 15, Michigan on Feb. 22, and Virginia on Feb. 29. Super Tuesday is scheduled for March 7.

The full DNC membership is expected to finalize the calendar at its next meeting in Austin, Texas, in August.

The early positioning comes six years after Buttigieg finished fifth in the 2020 Democratic presidential primary. Since then, he has remained one of the party’s most prominent potential presidential contenders, serving as transportation secretary under President Joe Biden.

The DNC’s calendar decision has also unfolded amid internal debate over the party’s presidential nominating process, with DNC Chairman Ken Martin urging Democrats to move quickly toward a final decision on the 2028 calendar.

news.title: Who will control the US Senate in 2026? Nine races to watch
news.text:
With less than three months until Election Day, the fight for control of the US Senate is entering a critical stretch, with nine states emerging as the contests most likely to determine which party controls the chamber next year.Democrats see an opening as President Donald Trump's approval rating and economic standing weaken. A recent CNN/SSRS poll put Trump's approval at 34%, while 65% of Americans said his policies had worsened economic conditions. Democrats also held an eight-point advantage on the generic congressional ballot.But the path to a Democratic majority remains difficult. Republicans currently hold the Senate, and Democrats need a net gain of four seats while protecting their own vulnerable incumbents.1. North CarolinaNorth Carolina remains Democrats' clearest opportunity to flip a Republican-held seat.Former Gov. Roy Cooper is facing Republican Michael Whatley in a race to replace retiring GOP Sen. Thom Tillis. Cooper's statewide political record and strong polling have made the contest a major Democratic target. CNN recently ranked the state as the Senate seat most likely to change hands.Live EventsA Fox News poll also showed Cooper with a nine-point advantage over Whatley, 53% to 44%, while Democrats held an enthusiasm edge.2. MaineRepublican Sen. Susan Collins faces another difficult reelection campaign in a state that backed Kamala Harris in 2024.Democrats' candidate changed late in the race after Graham Platner withdrew, with former state Senate President Troy Jackson becoming the party's nominee. A University of New Hampshire Survey Center poll conducted before Jackson formally secured the nomination showed him narrowly ahead of Collins, 49% to 46%.Collins' independent reputation could help her, but Democratic strategists see voter dissatisfaction with Trump as a potential opening.3. MichiganMichigan could be the race that determines whether Democrats can realistically reach the four-seat gain they need.Progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed emerged from a contentious primary and will face Republican Mike Rogers. His victory was a major win for the party's progressive wing, but his narrow primary margin leaves questions about whether he can consolidate moderate voters.Republicans are already portraying El-Sayed as too liberal for the battleground state, while Democrats are expected to make Trump's record and economic concerns central to their campaign.CNN's analysis has placed Michigan among the most important Republican pickup opportunities. 4. OhioFormer Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown is attempting a comeback against Republican Sen. Jon Husted.Ohio has shifted sharply toward Republicans in presidential elections, making Brown's challenge difficult. Still, his fundraising and statewide profile keep the race competitive.Recent political handicapping has moved Ohio toward the toss-up category, underscoring the state's importance to the Democratic strategy.5. AlaskaFormer Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola is challenging Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in another race Democrats hope can break their way.Alaska's open primary and ranked-choice voting system could make the November contest particularly unpredictable. CNN previously identified Peltola as one of the Democrats' strongest opportunities in a traditionally Republican state.6. IowaIowa could become essential to Democratic Senate math if Republicans manage to flip Michigan.Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson is facing Democrat Josh Turek, with economic issues likely to dominate the contest. Tariffs and their impact on farmers are emerging as major Democratic talking points in a state Trump won comfortably in 2024.CNN has highlighted Iowa as one of the deep-red states where Democrats nevertheless have a realistic pickup opportunity.7. TexasTexas is increasingly drawing attention as Democrat James Talarico challenges Republican Ken Paxton.The race has tightened in recent polling, while Talarico has built a substantial fundraising advantage. Republicans are expected to rely heavily on Trump's strength in the state, while Democrats are targeting economic concerns and Paxton's political baggage.The contest could become one of the biggest tests of whether Democrats can expand the Senate map beyond traditional battlegrounds.8. New HampshireThe race to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen remains competitive, with Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas and former Republican Sen. John E. Sununu expected to emerge as the leading candidates.New Hampshire's status as a swing state makes the race particularly important, but Trump's weak standing there could complicate Republican efforts to flip the seat.9. GeorgiaGeorgia rounds out the list despite Democrats holding the seat.Sen. Jon Ossoff is the only Democratic Senate incumbent running in a state Trump won in 2024, making him a prime Republican target. But Ossoff enters the race with a major financial and polling advantage over Republican Mike Collins.A Fox News poll released in July showed Ossoff leading Collins 56% to 43% among registered voters.Republicans are expected to spend heavily to close that gap, but Ossoff's fundraising operation gives Democrats considerable room to defend the seat.Why these races matterNorth Carolina, Maine, Michigan and Ohio currently offer Democrats their clearest routes toward a Senate majority, while Alaska, Iowa and Texas could become essential if the party loses ground elsewhere.The races are still fluid, and polling, fundraising and candidate momentum could dramatically reshape the map before November.For now, however, these nine contests provide the clearest picture of where the 2026 US Senate battle is likely to be won or lost.Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: Joe Scarborough slams Democrats for tolerating unhinged lefties: ‘Too woke to call out the obvious’
news.text:
“Morning Joe” host Joe Scarborough went on a fiery rant against Democrats, shouting that party leaders were permitting the most controversial voices to gain prominence because they are “too woke to call out the obvious.”

The MS Now show ran a clip of Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s (D-NY) Sunday appearance on ABC’s “This Week” in which she was pressed about her decision not to endorse Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist candidate in the Wisconsin gubernatorial race who once called for abolishing the police, prisons — and even Thanksgiving.

Ocasio-Cortez evaded the question, while rambling that Hong had “moved away” from many of those old positions. She then said a New York City councilman has a great line for it — “Woke 1 was crazy.”

Scarborough ripped into the congresswoman’s dismissive response, arguing that there’s “no great conspiracy” behind renewed criticism of the Democratic Socialists of America, citing the success of New York City’s far-left Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

The host praised Mamdani as someone who’s “proven to be, I think, extremely pragmatic in many ways,” while also calling out his high approval rating, the lowest murder rate “on record” and a “thriving” economy.

“But you also have [DSA] people in New York City that have been saying some whacked-out things,” Scarborough continued.

“I think most mainstream voters would say they’re whacked-out things, when they’re talking about going to pro-Hamas rallies the day after Hamas slaughtered more Jews than on any day since the Holocaust. I think 90% of Americans would think that is abhorrent.” he said.

“And so, you know, again, they’ll try to blur the lines – ‘Oh, well, they just don’t support healthcare for all’ – no, no, we’re not saying that. We just [don’t] support hate speech,” Scarborough continued.

The host then turned to the 2024 election, noting that Democrats failed to confront culturally divisive issues that Republicans were able to weaponized successfully against former Dem presidential candidate Kamala Harris.

“You couldn’t watch an NFL game without seeing 300, ‘Taxpayers are going to pay for trans surgeries for convicts’ ads,” he said, arguing that the messaging moved working-class male voters across all demographics toward President Trump.

He said that Democrats could campaign on an economic populist message, namely, higher taxes on billionaires and healthcare reform –“something that most Americans would agree with.”

“But please, I don’t need people telling me, ‘Oh, you have to just turn a blind eye to people saying that women getting raped on October 7 didn’t matter, in the grand scheme of things.’ No, Americans aren’t going to support that.”

He turned back to Ocasio-Cortez, saying she and the other Democrats are “once again fumbling the football on the two-yard line when they have a chance to make great gains but being so woke – I don’t know if you want to call it woke 1, woke 2 or woke 3 – but being too woke to call out the obvious!

“I swear to God, it’s really – it’s crazy that we’re even having this conversation!,” he shouted, before adding that Democratic leaders like Sen. Chuck Shumer and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York should be willing to call out extreme rhetoric and demand candidates distance themselves from it.

“We’re bringing this up now because it seems an awful lot like what was happening in 2024, when Democrats couldn’t get out of their own way to win an election they should have won!” Scarborough concluded.
news.summary: "Morning Joe" host Joe Scarborough went on a fiery rant against Democrats, shouting that party leaders were permitting the most controversial voices to gain prominence because they are "too woke to call out the obvious."

news.title: Trump's Pre-Midterm Approval Rating Compared to Biden, Obama and Bush
news.text: President Donald Trump’s approval rating ahead of the midterm elections sits at a lower point than other modern American presidents, according to polling data from the Pew Research Center and Quinnipiac University. Midterms are often seen as a referendum on a sitting president, so approval numbers are watched closely in the months leading up to those elections. Historically, when a president has a poor national approval rating, their party tends to lose seats in the midterms. Trump’s declining approval rating has driven Democratic hopes that they could retake a majority of seats in both the House of Representatives and the Senate. Trump isn’t alone in having a poor approval rating—polls showed nearly all 21st Century presidents underwater ahead of their midterms, with the exception of President George W. Bush in 2002, when Republicans were able to fend off a blue wave and actually pick up congressional seats. But the latest approval polls show him in a worse position than any recent president in the mid-to-late summer ahead of the midterms, a potential worrying sign for Republicans who have hoped to hold onto their majorities. Democrats have their challenges, as well, including polling that consistently shows poor favorability for the party. But many Democrats believe frustration with Trump over inflation and gas prices will be the key issue in November, even as Republicans seek to turn the midterms into a referendum on the rise of progressivism in the Democratic Party. Newsweek reached out to the White House for comment via email. Trump Approval Rating Compared to Biden, Bush and Obama Quinnipiac University and the Pew Research Center have consistently tracked presidential approval ratings across recent administrations and offer key insights into how Trump’s approval stacks up against his predecessors. The latest Quinnipiac poll, conducted among 963 registered voters from July 23-27, 2026, showed 32 percent of respondents approving of Trump, while 58 percent disapproving. That is a modern historical low for this point in a presidency for their polling. In August 2022, the pollster found that former President Joe Biden’s approval rating stood at 40 percent, while 52 percent disapproved. In August 2018, during Trump’s first term in office, his approval fared better with 41 percent approving and 54 percent disapproving. Former President Barack Obama’s approval was better in both of his terms. In June 2014, his approval stood at 40 percent and disapproval at 53 percent. In July 2010, just months before a major GOP wave in the midterms, his approval rating stood at 44 percent and disapproval at 48 percent. President Bush’s approval rating initially remained high due to his leadership following the September 11 terror attacks in 2001, though his favorability had waned by 2006 amid growing frustration over the Iraq War. In August 2006, 39 percent of respondents said they approved of Bush, compared to 53 percent who disapproved of him. In November 2002, a year after the attacks, 62 percent of respondents said they approved of Bush, compared to 30 percent who disapproved. Pew Research Center data show a similar story. In 2002, 67 percent of respondents said they approved of Bush. Obama’s approval stood at 47 percent in 2010, while Trump’s stood at 40 percent in 2018. In 2022, only 37 percent of respondents told Pew they approved of Biden. But Trump’s 2026 approval is still slightly worse at 34 percent in the latest July 13 numbers from the research center. How Have Congressional Races Gone in Recent Cycles? Republicans won control of the House in 2024 with less than a 2-point edge in the popular vote. They won 220 seats to the Democrats’ 215. They also won a Senate majority, flipping four races to hold a total of 53 seats. In 2022, the GOP won the popular vote by just under 3 points, securing 222 seats to the Democrats’ 213. However, the Democrats picked up one Senate seat to give them a majority with a total of 49 seats, along with two independents who caucus with the party. Democrats held a slim majority after the 2020 elections—222 seats to 213 while winning the popular vote by about 3 points. Democrats also picked up three Senate seats. They ended up with 48 seats plus two independents who caucus with Democrats, and then-Vice President Kamala Harris served as the tiebreaker. In 2018, the last blue wave, Democrats won 235 seats to the Republicans’ 199. They won the popular vote by nearly 9 points. However, Republicans were able to net two Senate seats, expanding their majority to give them a total of 53 seats. Two years earlier in 2016, Republicans won the House popular vote by only about a point while losing 6 seats to Democrats. Republicans still held a majority, 241 to 194. On the Senate side, Republicans lost two seats but still held a majority, with a total of 52 seats. In 2014, Republicans gained ground in both chambers, winning a 247-188 majority in the House while flipping 13 seats. In the Senate, Republicans flipped 9 seats to give them a total of 54 seats. In 2012, Democrats picked up 8 seats in the House, winning the popular vote by about a point. Republicans, however, still had a 234-201 majority. In the Senate, Democrats held a majority with 53 seats after flipping two GOP-held seats. Republicans had a very strong year in 2010, flipping a net of 63 House seats while winning the popular vote by nearly 7 points. Republicans also flipped six Senate seats, but Democrats still had a majority, holding a total of 51 seats, along with an additional two independents caucusing with them. Why Is Trump’s Approval Faltering? The economy is viewed as a major issue for Trump; Americans often vote based on who they believe will improve their material economic conditions, and polls regularly show economic issues as the top concern for voters. Trump campaigned on tackling affordability and inflation, issues emerging in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic—and his focus on economic issues helped propel his return to the White House. But as the midterms approach, inflation has remained elevated, and voters have shown they are increasingly frustrated over Trump’s approach to the economy. In the Quinnipiac poll, just 34 percent said they approved of Trump on the economy, down from 42 percent in January. Only 3 percent said they view the economy as being "excellent," while 25 percent say it is in "good" condition. Thirty percent said it is "not so good," while 41 percent said it is "poor." The Iran war is also unpopular with voters, with only 34 percent of respondents in the Quinnipiac poll saying they support the "U.S. military action against Iran," down from 40 percent in March. Gas prices have also increased during the war because of disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, a major passageway for the global oil supply, that has faced closures amid the conflict that began at the end of February. Costs topping $4 per gallon have caused pain at the pump for consumers and a major polling headache for Trump. Trump addressed his approval rating in a Truth Social post earlier in August. "My REAL Polling Numbers, not those made up by the Fake News Media, are the best they have ever been, and why wouldn’t they be with the biggest tax cuts and employment numbers EVER, the biggest outside Investment in America in World history, a totally secure Border, a giant Victory in Venezuela, the Denuclearization of Iran, unparalleled respect and success throughout the World, and much more?" he wrote. Democrats’ Chances of Flipping the House and Senate in Midterms Overall, prediction markets favored Democrats to flip the House as of Monday morning. Kalshi placed their chances of flipping the House at 85 percent, while Polymarket gave them an 89 percent chance. However, Republicans were still favored in the Senate, having a 54 percent chance of holding onto Congress’ upper chamber, while Polymarket gave them a 55 percent chance of holding onto their majority on Monday. Prediction markets allow traders to buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real‑money wagers into probability estimates. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment at a given moment but do not always accurately predict the future. Control of Congress could come down to just a handful of competitive races. In the Senate, the Cook Political Report shows the Senate races in Alaska, Maine, Michigan and Ohio as tossups. Meanwhile, there are 18 toss-up House races. What Happens Next? Trump’s approval rating will continue to be closely watched in the coming months as the midterms inch closer. Polling, fundraising and the national political environment in the coming weeks could offer key clues as to whether Trump's low approval rating translates into electoral losses for the GOP. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Trevor Davies.
news.summary: The President's position is worse than his predecessors before the November elections, according to two major pollsters.

news.title: Miss North Carolina USA Breaks Silence After Being Stripped of Her Title—And Replaced by her Black Runner-Up
news.text:
Former Miss North Carolina USA Brittany Boltinhouse is breaking her silence after having her title stripped away by the prestigious pageant system — and after the first runner-up, a Black woman named Myla Hadley, has now taken her place. 

If you missed it, here’s the background: Five weeks after Boltinhouse was crowned, her title was taken away following an internal investigation run by the organization. While their findings weren’t publicized, they did cite “conduct over an extended period of time” and noted in a statement that their decision wasn’t based on a “single moment.”

However, local North Carolina outlet NCBeat pointed to resurfaced tweets where Boltinhouse allegedly used the n-word frequently years ago, and more recently allegedly criticized former Vice President Kamala Harris and espoused conservative beliefs.

And while Miss USA CEO Thom Brodeur didn’t address those tweets or the post, he made it clear that the org doesn’t stand for or tolerate “racism, homophobia or transphobia.”

Related: New Book Reveals Miss USA’s Final Text Before Suicide, Mother’s Heartbreaking Response

“The Miss USA organization does not tolerate racism, homophobia, transphobia nor language that strips any person of their dignity—whoever they are. That is not a policy written for a press release. It is the floor of what it means to represent this brand,” Brodeur said in an official statement to Instagram.

He later added: “A title here isn’t a trinket. It is a position of trust, extended by an organization and accepted by a woman who agrees to carry a standard in public. When that standard is broken, the title cannot continue as though nothing happened.”

Boltinhouse has now decided to speak out about the ordeal. Specifically, she sat down for an on-camera interview with The Carolina Journal, where she revealed that she felt her title was taken away from her due to her conservative beliefs.

“All I can say is that I think and believe that my title was ripped from me because of my beliefs,” she told the outlet.

She later added: “I am a member of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints. I am proud of my faith. I’m proud of my standards. I’m a proud conservative woman, but a Christian woman. I’m a God-fearing woman. I will never let my guard down for my faith.”

Boltinhouse went on to say that while the decision was a “huge shock,” she views it as a “blessing in disguise.” However, when asked about those aforementioned social media posts, she dismissed them, chalking them up to simple “mistakes.”

Now, former Tennessee State University student Myla Hadley will take her spot and compete in the Miss USA competition set to go down later this month. Taking to Instagram, the former HBCU student shared words of gratitude and support for those in her corner now and assured those watching that she’d be ready to represent the state of North Carolina well, in spite of the last-minute shakeup.

“Thank you to everyone for all the support and love you’ve shown me throughout this entire process,” Hadley wrote on Instagram. “I understand the seriousness and level of prestige that this title carries, and I can confidently say that both my team and I are ready to take this on.”

She concluded: “While this may seem like a two-week turnaround given the circumstances, I’ve been preparing to represent at Miss USA since I first competed with this organization. I am ready to represent North Carolina.”

Judging by Hadley’s latest Instagram post where she finally picked out the dress she’ll be competing in, it looks like she’s already on her way to doing just that.

news.text: Conservatives piled on former Vice President Kamala Harris after she warned Americans would have to "prove who you are" under the SAVE America Act, arguing her criticism inadvertently turned into a sales pitch for the Republican-backed bill. "Incredible SAVE America Act saleswoman," wrote conservative commentator Eric Daughetry on X. Harris posted a video on her X account Friday discussing midterm elections while highlighting the SAVE Act, including lamenting to voters that "you’re going to have to have proof of who you are." She added the bill will require "a passport, which a lot of Americans don’t have, or a birth certificate. Same point, obstacles to make it difficult for you to register to vote." The clip went viral among conservatives, with Trump even pinning the video to the top of his profile on Truth Social. "The Jim Crow comparisons are tired. The poll tax is gone. Jim Crow is gone. REPUBLICAN SAYS TRUMP'S TOP ELECTION PRIORITY 'DEAD' IN SENATE AS GOP FRACTURES AHEAD OF MIDTERMS Trump has warned about the need for voter ID laws for years, including from the 2016 campaign trail. With Congress out of session and the midterms approaching, Trump is continuing to push lawmakers to prioritize passage of the SAVE Act, keeping pressure on Republicans to act when they return to Washington. news.title: Joe Scarborough Thinks Democrats Are ‘Fumbling the Football on the 2-Yard Line’ Ahead of Midterms
news.text:
“Morning Joe” host Joe Scarborough slammed elected Democrats on Monday morning for refusing to denounce the extremist views of some of the party’s most contentious figures this year, arguing that the political party is “fumbling the football at the two-yard line” just like it did in 2024.

The subject of the Monday morning segment was Wisconsin state assemblywoman and gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America who previously called for the police to be abolished and for Thanksgiving to be cancelled. Scarborough, for his part, marveled at mainstream Democrats’ reluctance to distance themselves from candidates like Hong.

“The Democratic Party has a choice to make,” Scarborough explained. “I said this day-in and day-out leading up to Kamala Harris’ election. You couldn’t watch an NFL game without seeing 300 ‘Taxpayers are going to pay for trans surgeries for convicts’ ads on NFL games.”

“Even though [Democrats] still pretend that did not move viewers, I think the Trump campaign spent $30 million on those ads, and it moved working class men, working class white men, working class Black men, working class Hispanic men,” the MS NOW host noted. “It just did, and the Democrats had their head in the sand.”

“This is not about me,” the former Republican Florida congressman added. “This is about the Democrats, once again, fumbling the football on the two-yard line when they have a chance to make great gains, but being … too woke to call out the obvious. I swear to God, it’s really crazy that we’re even having this conversation.”

Scarborough argued that Democrats need to focus on promoting candidates with mainstream economic views during this year’s midterm election cycle, rather than siding with candidates who have extremist social and anti-Israel positions.

“There’s nothing wrong with the Democrats supporting economic justice. There’s nothing wrong with the Democrats supporting cutting taxes, or getting rid of the Trump taxes and making billionaires pay more,” he said. “That’s a legitimate mainstream debate for people to have. Health care for all! Health care is unaffordable. That is something most Americans would agree with.”

“I don’t need people telling me, ‘Oh, you have to just turn a blind eye to people saying that women getting raped on Oct. 7 didn’t matter in the grand scheme of things.’ Americans aren’t going to support that,” Scarborough continued. “If somebody [talks about] going to a [pro-Hamas] rally the day after Hamas slaughters more Jews than any time since the Holocaust, it’s OK for Chuck Schumer, it’s OK for Hakeem Jeffries to call that despicable and demand that people distance themselves from that.”

“Why are we bringing this up now?” he asked in conclusion. “Because it seems an awful lot like what was happening in 2024 when Democrats couldn’t get out of their own way to win an election they should have won!”

news.title: Donald Trump's 'dinner outburst showed true feelings about Melania,' ex-aide says
news.text: Melania Trump's noticeable absence from her husband Donald's side has become increasingly evident as his second term unfolds. A former advisor believes Trump revealed his true sentiments towards his wife during a heated tirade at a White House dinner. As reported by the Daily Beast, the First Lady has only made 38 public appearances in the first seven months of 2026. She was also reportedly seen in public just 47 times in 2025 following the inauguration on January 20. This is a stark contrast when compared to the likes of Michelle Obama, Jill Biden and Laura Bush. There has subsequently been intense speculation about the state of their relationship. Anthony Scaramucci, who infamously served as Trump's White House Communications Director for a mere 11 days at the beginning of his first term, found himself on the receiving end of a shocking outburst from the President over seating arrangements, reports the Mirror US . Anthony informed the Daily Beast's podcast that he had always maintained a positive relationship with Melania, sharing a "good rapport" with the First Lady. This seemed to irk Trump, who showed his true colours when Anthony and Melania ended up seated next to each other during a dinner in the White House's Blue Room. He stated: "For some reason I was sitting next to Melania. And he got pissed at me. "He's a taller guy than me. And he looked over and looked down at me and he's like: 'Why are you sitting next to my wife?' "And I looked at him and I'm like: 'I have no idea. First of all, do you think I made the place cards? I have no idea why I'm sitting next to your wife.' "And I think it unnerves him when people have a good rapport with her." The political adviser revealed that once Trump realised Anthony had played no part in the seating arrangements, he settled down. Anthony had originally been critical of Trump before ultimately supporting him in the 2016 election, joining the campaign's finance committee and transition team. He then endured his short-lived spell as Communications Director in July 2017. Within days of starting the role, he launched a scathing assault on Trump administration members during an interview with The New Yorker that he thought was off the record. He was swiftly dismissed. Anthony is now a vocal opponent of Trump, backing Democratic candidates Joe Biden in 2020 and Kamala Harris in 2024. Speaking about his relationship with Melania, he revealed: "She was always very nice to me. I always liked her, my wife liked her. She was down to earth, classy." Anthony has previously spoken about Melania's relationship with her husband, alleging she privately wished Kamala Harris would defeat Trump in the 2024 election. He even suggested that she "hated" her husband.
news.summary: Former White House advisor Anthony Scaramucci believes Donald Trump's angry reaction at a White House dinner showed his true feelings towards the First Lady Melania

news.title: Nate Jackson: The Burrito Food Fight on the Right
news.text:
Can you afford a burrito? An argument over the answer to that question took off among conservatives last week, and it might be the defining question of the 2026 election. Republicans are losing ground with voters on the economy. While Democrats caused the inflation problem, they stand to benefit from harping on “affordability” in the midterms.

President Donald Trump was elected to do two things: Fix the immigration crisis and stop inflation. Both crises were creations of Joe Biden’s administration, and millions of Americans understood the solution to both was to say “no” to Kamala “The Biden Clone” Harris and “yes” to Donald Trump.

Trump has clearly solved immigration. The border is effectively closed, as there are virtually no illegal alien crossings now. Trump is also deporting many illegals from the interior, and he’s not giving up the fight on birthright citizenship. Overall, I’d give him an A on the issue.

Unfortunately, the economy is another matter. He began a love affair with tariffs, which are taxes that raise the price of goods. And he launched a war in Iran, which caused wide and generally upward fluctuations in oil prices. Both tariffs and the war are meant to achieve arguably necessary objectives, but both have hurt Americans’ budgets, and both could cost Republicans in November.

The burrito argument began, as many things do, on social media. “Grocery prices are insane,” posted The Daily Wire’s Matt Walsh. “They’re still rising. Addressing this problem should be the number one priority of every elected leader. End the stupid foreign wars and focus on this issue. It’s one of the main reasons socialists are gaining power.”

TPUSA’s Andrew Kolvet, who has largely become the face of the organization after Charlie Kirk’s murder, responded, “One of our TPUSA college students gave me his take on affordability: ‘A burrito shouldn’t cost $20.’ Yeah, a lot of this is a hangover from Covid and Biden-era inflation, but the lived experience is the same: It just feels like basic things cost too much.”

I know food is expensive, but nobody has to pay $20 for a burrito. As The Daily Wire’s Ben Shapiro asserted, “If you’re paying $20 for a burrito and you’re not independently wealthy, you’re doing life wrong.”

The same thoughts occurred to many other conservatives, who argued about everything from college meal plans to making your own burritos to noting that groceries represent a smaller portion of most family budgets than they used to — 9.7% today versus 12% in 1985. That’s likely more a function of other budget items than grocery prices.

Former George W. Bush speechwriter Marc Thiessen essentially defended the Trump administration’s economic record, and Vice President JD Vance personally insulted him for it: “If you’ve ever met him in person, it’s quite obvious the man has never missed a burrito.” A lot of Americans could probably do with fewer burritos, but maybe that’s beside the point.

The ones arguing facts are right on the merits, but they’re completely whiffing on the sentiment, which, as Walsh said, is why the Democratic Socialists are winning. Young Americans are coming out of college and struggling to land a decent job — never mind buying a grossly overpriced house with a high interest rate. They are unlikely to be swayed by the “suck it up, Buttercup” argument of the conservatives scoffing about burrito prices.

I’ll readily note what many of you from older generations are thinking: Many young people are struggling precisely because they didn’t grow up hearing “suck it up, Buttercup.” If young people hadn’t been coddled, they’d be tougher and more ready for the world. They’d be happier if they didn’t expect to graduate from college, immediately make six figures, and order gourmet organic food from DoorDash. I’ll also note that even 9.1% inflation under Joe Biden didn’t match what Americans dealt with in the late 1970s and early ‘80s.

It’s also true that not everything is guac and salsa right now.

“The typical American’s paycheck has grown faster since 2019 than in any stretch since the early 1980s,” reports CBS News. “But prices climbed nearly as fast. Consumer costs rose 30% over the same seven years, swallowing about 80% of the typical worker’s raise. What survives is roughly $70 more a week to spend in today’s dollars. That’s about 6% over seven years or a gain of less than 1% a year.”

That’s why it just feels like burritos cost too much.

Taco Bell has been in the news for other hilariously undesirable reasons of late, but I’ll use the fast food chain as an example. In 2019, a burrito supreme cost $3.89. That same menu item is now $5.99, or about 53% more expensive. Most Americans haven’t gotten a 53% raise since 2019.

More generally, food is a lot more expensive than it was when Trump left office the first time. There are a lot of reasons for that, virtually all of which are the direct results of Democrat policies. For example, 19 states raised the minimum wage this year, which makes burritos more expensive. But voters blame the party in power, and right now, that’s the GOP.

Republicans have a much harder argument to make, even if it’s correct. Conservatives advocate personal responsibility, as we should, but that’s less attractive than the DSA’s pitch of Free Stuff™. Joe Biden learned that telling voters inflation wasn’t happening was a terrible strategy. Similarly, if Republicans want to win, they better figure out how to connect with voters on their biggest concern — the economy as represented by the price of a burrito.

They can start by hammering home that socialism will lead to burrito lines.

news.title: Alabama Special Congressional Primaries: What’s at Stake
news.text:
WASHINGTON – Alabama voters in four of the state’s seven congressional districts head to the polls Tuesday to choose U.S. House nominees under a newly drawn map that removes one of the two majority-Black districts now represented by Democrats.

The state had initially planned to hold primaries for all seven congressional seats on May 19. But Republican Gov. Kay Ivey delayed voting in the 1st, 2nd, 6th and 7th Congressional Districts after a U.S. Supreme Court ruling set off a wave of map changes in several Republican-led Southern states.

Those court-driven revisions in Alabama, Louisiana and Tennessee — along with earlier mid-decade redistricting moves elsewhere — formed part of a broader Republican push, backed by President Donald Trump, to improve the party’s odds of protecting its narrow U.S. House majority in the 2026 midterm elections.

Alabama’s current House delegation will remain in place under the existing district lines through the end of 2026. The candidates competing in Tuesday’s primaries, however, are seeking nominations in districts shaped by the new Republican-supported map, which takes effect in January 2027. The state’s two Democratic members of Congress are both running for reelection in their redrawn districts and face no primary opposition.

The changes are especially significant in the 2nd District, where U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures is seeking a second term. Black residents make up about half of the current district’s population, but that share would fall to roughly 40% under the new boundaries. In the 2024 presidential race, Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris carried the current district over Trump, 53% to 46%. Under the new map, Trump would have won the district instead, 57% to 42%.

Six Republicans are competing for the chance to face Figures in November. The field includes state Rep. Rhett Marques, Army veteran Joshua McKee and real estate broker Hampton Harris. Trump has thrown his support behind Marques, who has also led the Republican field in fundraising.

In the newly configured 7th District, Black residents would retain a narrow majority. U.S. Rep. Terri Sewell is running there for a ninth term. Harris defeated Trump in the current version of the district, 61% to 38%, and would still have prevailed under the new lines, though by a smaller margin of 58% to 41%. Republicans Ammie Akin and David Perry are vying for the nomination to challenge Sewell.

Below are key details about the Alabama congressional primaries and the data points the AP Decision Team will be watching as results come in.

When do polls close?

Polls close at 7 p.m. CT, which is 8 p.m. ET.

What’s on the ballot?

The Associated Press will provide vote results and declare winners in contested primaries for the 1st, 2nd, 6th and 7th Congressional Districts.

Who gets to vote?

The special primaries are open to any registered voters in their respective congressional districts. Although Alabama does not register voters by party, voters will be asked to declare a party preference upon selecting a party’s primary ballot.

How many voters are there?

As of June 1, there were 3.8 million registered voters in Alabama. Each congressional district in the state has a total population of about 718,000.

How many people actually vote?

About 409,000 ballots were cast across the state in the May 19 primaries, which was roughly 11% of registered voters. Past vote totals for the four new congressional districts are unavailable.

How much of the vote is cast early or by absentee ballot? 

Relatively few Alabama voters cast their ballots before Election Day. The state is one of the only holdouts in the country not to offer some form of in-person early voting. In the 2024 primaries, about 4% of Democratic primary voters and about 1% of Republican primary voters voted by mail.

When are early and absentee votes released?

Vote release practices vary from county to county. Most counties tend to release results from absentee voting in the first vote update, sometimes along with results from in-person Election Day voting.

How long does vote-counting usually take?

In the May 19 state primary, the AP first reported results at 8:28 p.m. ET, or 28 minutes after polls closed. The last vote update of the night was at 12:54 a.m. ET, with more than 99.9% of total votes counted.

When will the AP declare a winner?

The AP does not make projections and will declare a winner only when it’s determined there is no scenario that would allow a trailing candidate to close the gap. If a race has not been called, the AP will continue to cover any newsworthy developments, such as candidate concessions or declarations of victory. In doing so, the AP will make clear that it has not yet declared a winner and explain why.

How do recounts work?

In 2010, the Alabama attorney general issued an opinion that Alabama’s automatic recount law does not apply to primaries. The AP may declare a winner in a race that is subject to a recount if it can determine the lead is too large for a recount or legal challenge to change the outcome.

Are we there yet?

As of Tuesday, there will be 84 days until the 2026 midterm elections.

news.text:
At the "Masquerade Sneaker Ball" in New Orleans on Friday, Kamala, for some reason, was the keynote attraction. She railed against what she called a "broken status quo," complained about "millions in dark money" flowing into politics (apparently only when it funds the other team), and lectured her party on the importance of knowing how to fight.

Then came the part that really perked me up. Kamala said Democrats need to get "comfortable" adopting a certain "ruthlessness" going forward. She described the posture she wants for her party as one "that fights back hard when they threaten the power of the people." I know, I rolled my eyes, too. Nothing Democrats have ever done has been for the people, but for their own power. Still, this is exactly the kind of language you'd expect from someone hoping her base fills in the blanks with whatever level of aggression makes them feel best.

The Democratic Party needs to get comfortable with a certain kind of ruthlessness. pic.twitter.com/wbJSSb3cJF— Kamala Harris (@KamalaHarris) August 8, 2026

Let's stop pretending Democrats don't already fight hard.

This is the same party that treated the filibuster as sacred when it blocked George W. Bush's judicial nominees, insisting it protected the minority party's voice, then nuked it under Harry Reid the moment Republicans used the same tool against Barack Obama. Consistency was never the point. Winning was.

ICYMI: The Most Bizarre Thing That Has Been Discovered About Fauci's Phone So Far

And then there's Donald Trump. Democrats impeached him twice on the flimsiest of pretexts, and they're already promising more investigations and another likely impeachment attempt. The Biden administration even tried to put him in prison to keep him out of the White House altogether. And for good measure, they attempted a federal takeover of elections to keep their party in power permanently. How much more ruthless does a political party need to get before Kamala notices they've already crossed every line she's pretending to draw?

Then there's the dangerous rhetoric. Democrats have called Trump a Nazi, a dictator, and an existential threat to democracy so often the label has practically lost meaning, except to the people who took it seriously enough to try to kill him. Multiple times. A radicalized lunatic murdered Charlie Kirk after being brainwashed by exactly this kind of language. Democrats don't have a deficit of ruthlessness. They have a ruthlessness surplus, and Kamala just asked for more.

So why is she saying this now? Why do Democrats do anything? Power.

Early 2028 polling has often shown her leading the field of Democrat contenders. But as I’ve said before, that lead is a mirage built on name recognition, not enthusiasm, and Kamala knows it better than anyone after 2024. What she's really doing is auditioning for a base that thinks the party hasn't been vicious enough. She's not describing a new strategy. She's flattering the people who already think Democrats are too polite, hoping their anger becomes her 2028 launchpad. The far-left base. The socialists. The activists that the establishment is afraid of.
