news.title: GOP midterm strategy embraces Trump’s ‘communism’ fixation
news.text:
Painting Democrats as communists wouldn’t have been their first choice. But current and former White House aides welcome the midterm election strategy that President Donald Trump has concocted — especially as administration officials have struggled to defend Trump’s economic policies in his second term. 

“Where things are at right now, Trump’s record doesn’t really get the base too excited,” a former aide to President Donald Trump told MS NOW, acknowledging that “if you look at what voters care about right now, Trump doesn’t have a lot to boast of.”

“The GOP right now is smart to point to Democrats who are struggling with their identity,” said the former aide, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly about the president’s record.

After a wave of democratic socialist primary wins, the president has settled on a midterm message that conflates democratic socialism with communism. Trump has called communism “the greatest threat to our country,” and he’s aiming to convince voters that the Democratic Party is that threat — much as he used the moniker against Kamala Harris in 2024.

His aides haven't corrected him, and after a year of private frustration that the president wasn’t focused enough on the midterms, they've welcomed the hyperbole and folded it into their political operation. 

“‘Democrats are communists’ isn’t exactly our rallying cry, but if it keeps Trump actually focused and talking about midterms, we’ll take it,” said a Republican political operative familiar with midterm strategy granted anonymity to speak about internal dynamics. 

Trump’s team isn’t new at figuring out how to work around him. Multiple Republican midterm political operatives have described a long-standing two-lane approach to midterm messaging. And one of them put it: “There’s what Trump says. And then there’s what we want candidates to say.” 

“We are encouraging candidates to contrast themselves to their opponents as much as possible,” said another Republican political operative familiar with the White House midterm strategy.

But the president's “communism” line has become too useful, and too loud, to ignore.

Next month, Republicans will host a first-of-its-kind midterm convention in Dallas, Texas, replete with marathon videography that will “100 percent" lean into the communist label that Trump has been utilizing, a person familiar with the convention planning said.

As Trump faces wilting approval numbers amid soaring prices and an unpopular war with Iran, a key convention focus will be — not on Trump’s record — but on highlighting and degrading fresh faces in the left wing of the Democratic Party. Those will include Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan, according to another person familiar with the convention planning, even though El-Sayed is not a democratic socialist. 

On Friday, Trump said the Republican Party’s fate this November is not necessarily his problem, telling Punchbowl News that voter anger is not aimed at him. 

“They're angry at Republicans,” Trump said. “But they're not angry at me. They're not angry at me, but they are angry at Republicans.”

Pressed on his lack of campaigning for GOP congressional candidates this cycle, Trump suggested that his 2024 victory seemingly precludes him from focusing on the midterms. “I said to somebody, ‘Wait a minute. You don't understand. I won. I'm not campaigning,’” he said, adding that recent travel to Nevada and Los Angeles to make speeches was optional. “I could do a lot easier.”

Crying “communism” isn’t new for Trump — “All we have to do is define our opponent as being a communist or a socialist or somebody who is going to destroy our country," Trump said in August 2024 — but he has escalated the theme over the past few months. 

The inflection point came on June 23, when a slate of democratic socialist candidates won New York Democratic primaries. Shortly after, during a July 3 speech at Mount Rushmore, Trump referenced communism over a dozen times, calling it “the greatest threat to our country, including World War I, World War II, Pearl harbor or even 9/11.” 

And since then, Trump has referred to communism in speeches or online over 100 times, according to an analysis by MS NOW. And there’s good reason why. A survey conducted by Echelon Insights, a GOP research firm, shows that 52% of voters have a negative view of socialism. And 53% of independent voters, a coveted voting bloc, had an unfavorable view of democratic socialism. A June Economist/YouGov poll revealed similar findings, with 40% of independent voters saying they would not support a Democratic socialist candidate. 

The Democrats' “path to a majority is getting narrower and narrower because of candidates like [democratic socialists],” one of the people familiar with convention planning said, “even though they thought this was a slam dunk for them.”

In a social media post late Sunday afternoon, Trump showcased his midterm tactics: “Black and Brown Voters don’t want Communism or Socialism — Not surprisingly, they are flocking to the Republican Party!”
news.author: Zeeshan Aleem

news.title: Democratic socialists revile Trump. But they blame Democrats for his return.
news.text:
CHICAGO — Among democratic socialists, Donald Trump is seen as a symptom of a dire political system, a liar and a failure of a president twice over. 

And there’s an understanding that he took advantage of the Democratic Party’s failures and a sense of abandonment from the working class that helped his rise and return. 

“You can't deny that if Democrats had delivered, if people had been taken care of, I don't think that Donald Trump would be back in office,” said JP Lyninger, a democratic socialist and local elected official in Louisville, Kentucky.

The blame directed at “the establishment” by the Democratic Socialists of America faithful is meant to be a harsh rebuke that Democrats' approach is flawed and broken after a decade of Trump dominating politics even when he isn’t in power. But for whatever opportunity that gives democratic socialism, there’s a clear risk at alienating people that already have a poor view of the Democratic Party as weak and out of touch. 

The democratic socialist blame game

This is a nation where a real estate mogul and former reality television star leads a party whose conservative ruling class once laughed him off, where the opposition managed to beat Trump a single time before divisions over age, electability and aid for Israel fractured coalitions and helped the former president return to power even after he tried to overturn a free and fair election. 

All this has given the DSA a delicate path out of the fringes. 

“People have become disillusioned with a party that has failed to prevent this sort of fascist insurgency within American politics, not just once, but now two times,” said Bobby Nichols, a DSA member who serves on the city council in Tempe, Arizona. “And there's a lot of concern that they're not going to be able to prevent it going forward.”

The Democratic Socialists of America has been legitimized by a series of flashy wins since Trump regained office after the 2024 election. Victory in the New York City mayor’s race by defeating a disgraced centrist former governor. Ousting a congressional incumbent in that city during a primary, as well as in Denver, not because of outright scandal but the prospect of being responsible for political malaise. 

What’s applauded in liberal enclaves, however, carries the danger of being alarming elsewhere, especially at a time when the scourges of antisemitism and Islamophobia are well apparent around the country. Those running in overwhelmingly blue districts don’t necessarily “have the appreciation for what the electorate looks like in purple states like mine,” said Chris Pappas, a Democratic New Hampshire congressman campaigning for the U.S. Senate this fall. 

“You’ve got to deliver a message that is unifying, that brings people together, that focuses on how you can put some wins on the board for voters,” he said. 

The DSA’s aberrant ambitions outline wanting to “draft a new constitution” and establishing “public ownership of the largest corporations and essential industries” in the name of accountability. 

They maintain they are looking out for the working class and promote the idea of a 32-hour work week along with housing and healthcare for all. 

But an aspect of their policy vision calls for the near impossible goal of abolishing the U.S. Senate and dramatically reigning in the power of the American presidency. 

At the same time, they’re relying on Democratic primaries, part of the system they are deeply skeptical of, to win Congressional seats. 

“The Democratic Party, whenever they put someone in office, is fundamentally a nicer face to pretty much what a lot of Republicans are doing anyways,” said Cerena Ermitanio, a DSA leader in Texas. 

Swapping elderly President Joe Biden out as the 2024 nominee for Kamala Harris after a maligned debate performance did not save Democrats from another four years of Trump. And there are democratic socialists in the movement who chose not to take a side. 

Sara Almosawi, national co-chair of the Young Democratic Socialists of America, called former Vice President Harris, “a corporate Democrat” with responsibility for “the worst thing I've ever seen in my life, the genocide of Palestinians in Gaza,” and called her “a Democrat that refused to work for working people.” 

“And then I had Trump, an incredibly racist billionaire, and I knew that the two-party system had made this happen, and I did not feel compelled to vote in either election for either of these candidates,” she said, also warning “if the party chooses another corporate Democrat to run again, it's not going to work out.” 

Mainstream anxiety

The DSA’s growth over the last decade is tied in with progressive leader Bernie Sanders' 2016 and 2020 presidential campaigns. And its victories this year have inspired unease. At a time when Democrats are trying to show Republicans don’t have the sole claim to patriotism in politics, having fights over how the nation should conduct itself in such an existential way comes with its own clear friction. 

Republicans, having been rocked by their own fringes over the years, have already taken to stereotyping Democrats across the partisan spectrum as part of a far out ilk. 

“What we see is time and again, the Democrat Party is electing radicals. But that's where the Democratic Party is today,” said Wisconsin GOP Rep. Bryan Steil. 

This all comes as Democrats have limited influence in Washington, though that could change just a few weeks from now where they have a realistic map to winning control of the House in this fall’s midterms, and taking back the Senate is a difficult, but not impossible, task. 

Before that even has a chance to happen, there’s already an eagerness for the handful of democratic socialists headed to Congress to test their influence once they get there, and potentially try and prevent New York Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries from becoming the next speaker of the House. 

“He doesn’t have anything to run on. He just runs on empty promises. And I wouldn’t even say he’s promising anything. I couldn’t tell you what his platform even is, besides just being a Democrat,” said Matthew Smith, who knocked doors and helped democratic socialist Darializa Avila Chevalier win against a congressional incumbent in New York earlier this year. “That’s all they run on, so I view him as an incredibly weak leader, and partially the reason that we see the rise of facism that we have today.” 

After seeing several of his own members lose to DSA-backed candidates this year, Jeffries public attention is on the midterms. During a speech in Pennsylvania recently, the man who could soon become the first Black Speaker of the House said that “unlike the MAGA Republicans, the Democratic Party is not a cult of personality,” and if his party wins “a Congress that stands up to an out-of-control president.” 

The complicated path ahead 

A major loss can lead a party’s voters to side with the unexpected. For Republicans, eight years of the nation’s first Black president and losses from two moderate styled GOP nominees against him gave way to Trump’s takeover. Democrats answered by picking their oldest nominee ever, and running campaigns that tried to win over distressed former Republicans. 

That’s not the kind of tact the DSA is interested in. And so far, its prominent figures have the luxury of focusing on purity rather than having to worry about pragmatism. Compromise means incremental change, if change at all. And their goals lean more towards the aspirational than the attainable. 

The DSA’s momentum is already facing limits and there’s sensitivity within their ranks to any perception that they are the weirdos of the political scene. 

After victories in starkly blue districts in Pennsylvania, New York and Colorado, the start of August brought a win in a Detroit-area congressional primary for the movement, as well as a loss for a controversial former congresswoman who tried to win back her old St. Louis seat. And ahead of Tuesday’s primaries in Wisconsin, a state Trump narrowly carried two years ago, a democratic socialist has become her party’s front runner in the race for governor. 

“This is not a socialist country and they embrace it at their peril,” said Wisconsin Rep. Tom Tiffany, running for the same statewide office on the Republican side. 

The resistance flair of the 2018 midterms during Trump’s first term in the White House has given way to a grim view eight years later that leaders on the left haven’t met the moment in a meaningful way. That they have lost the thread when it comes to building and winning against an opponent who threw away the rules of engagement long before he was ever sworn into office. 

Not being Trump is simply not enough. 

Yet Democrats worrying about their base shifting too far to the left and angering the people they need to win in the midterms and beyond already see omens. 

Rallying the DSA one night during a party gathering in Chicago, Illinois, Robert Levertis Bell, running for a state house seat in a reliably blue part of Kentucky, drew cheers from allies even as he conjured critics’ worst fears about the movement. 

“We are going to democratize this shitty little country,” Bell said.

news.title: The populist left has a theory. We're all about to test it.
news.text:
Last week, before his victory in Michigan's extraordinarily bitter Democratic Senate primary, I asked Abdul El-Sayed how he planned to bring the party together if he won.

The campaign pit El-Sayed, a progressive public health official backed by Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, not just against Rep. Haley Stevens, but also against much of the state's Democratic establishment. The centrist Stevens was supported by Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, Sen. Gary Peters and Attorney General Dana Nessel, among many others. She was also backed by tens of millions of dollars in outside spending, much of it by pro-Israel donors, in a race that was widely seen as a referendum on the Democratic Party's direction.

With all the bad feelings the primary engendered, I figured El-Sayed would need to make some overtures before November. Rep. Hillary Scholten, a Democrat, had refused to commit to voting for him in part because of his decision to campaign with leftist streamer Hasan Piker, who expresses jejune sympathies for all sorts of brutal anti-American regimes, Hamas among them. I wanted to know how he'd tried to persuade people like her.

El-Sayed didn't accept the premise that there were many people like her. "There's this operational sense of the party that says that elites carry constituents," he said. "If that was true, I'd lose. It's just not true. The only thing that has been driving any support for our opposition has been the $60 million of lies being put on TV."

That sounded rather strong. (The only thing?) I asked, "Do you really not believe that there are people whose opposition to your ideas, or skepticism of your ideas, is sincere?"

"I think there are really quite few," he replied.

Perhaps there are more than he thought. Given the forces arrayed against him, El-Sayed's victory, which was called Wednesday morning, is a remarkable accomplishment, and evidence of widespread Democratic distrust in their party leaders. But after polls predicted a double-digit blowout, it ended up being a narrow win: less than a single point, as of this writing.

These results are likely to panic Democrats who were already anxious about El-Sayed's electability. It's one thing to charge into a general election with an unconventional candidate who has an overwhelming voter mandate, another with one who didn't even hit 50%. But they also give El-Sayed, who has never before run against a Republican, a chance to recalibrate. He has so many skills as a politician: He's quick, magnetic, overflowing with infectious confidence. But he also has a blind spot, one endemic to his movement: an inability to grasp how and why people of good faith might see the world differently.

Like Sanders before him, El-Sayed seems to assume that there's a hidden reservoir of voters hungry for progressive populist policies, if only they can be reached and mobilized. On Monday, he described his campaign to me as the test of this hypothesis.

As he sees it, conventional wisdom is fundamentally mistaken about how to win his state, which voted for Donald Trump in 2016 and 2024.

"We have this outdated model that everybody moves on a continuum from left to right," El-Sayed said. Establishment Democrats assume the path to victory lies in staking out an ideological middle ground.

"I have an alternative hypothesis," he said. "That people so hate the establishment on both sides of the aisle that they were willing to hold their nose and vote for Donald Trump twice, because if this really was a moderate state, Donald Trump is no moderate." That would mean that the best person to take on the Republican Senate nominee, Mike Rogers — a multimillionaire former member of Congress known for his friendliness to Big Pharma — is a populist outsider like El-Sayed.

"People are really pissing mad, really, really pissing mad," he said. "They don't trust Democrats because they don't feel like Democrats are actually going to fight for the things that Democrats say they want to fight for."

I was skeptical of this hypothesis before Tuesday. (For one thing, polls showed that, astonishing as it may seem, voters regarded Trump as more moderate than either Hillary Clinton or Kamala Harris.) I'm more skeptical of it now. I would very much like to believe in the story El-Sayed is telling, because it would mean that progressives can win political power without making ideological sacrifices. But there isn't much evidence of a candidate as left-wing as El-Sayed winning a purple state. And while one premise of his campaign was that he could speak to disaffected working-class voters, in the primary, he, like many progressive candidates before him, did best in more affluent and educated areas.

But as high as the stakes are in this race — it could decide control of the Senate — it may be better to test his theory now, before the 2028 presidential election. Since the liberal, consensus candidate Mallory McMorrow dropped out of the Democratic Senate race in July, Michigan was bound to be a gamble either way, because the passionately pro-Israel Stevens had her own electability challenges. At least now we might resolve an argument that's been tearing at the Democratic Party since 2016, when Sanders lost the primary to Clinton.

Ever since then, many progressives have been seething at a Democratic establishment that, as they see it, has used electability arguments as a cudgel against the left and then failed to get elected. "Bernie would have won in a landslide," said Shawn Fain, head of the United Auto Workers union and a vocal El-Sayed backer. "Unfortunately, the establishment couldn't get out of the damn way in '16, and we ended up where we ended up."

On Tuesday, left-wing populists won the chance to see if their electoral theory holds. Either El-Sayed wins and shows anxious liberals like me new horizons of political possibility, or he loses in a year when Democrats are expected to dominate and offers a hard lesson on the necessity of pragmatism.

When you watch El-Sayed campaign, it's easy to see why he inspires so much excitement. The clips of him that go viral sometimes show him being arrogant or insulting, and there's clearly a belligerent side to his personality. But he's also charming, wonky and skilled at uplift. In 2007, when he was valedictorian of his class at the University of Michigan, he shared a stage with Bill Clinton. His speech was so good that even though he was headed to medical school, Clinton urged him to consider a career in public service.

On Monday evening in Detroit, El-Sayed gave the final speech of his primary campaign, addressing volunteers at the Congregation, a former church that's been turned into a coffee shop and event space. He emphasized what America had given him as the son of Egyptian immigrants. "I love America because I know exactly what my life should have been but for the accident of history that allowed me to be born in America," he said. He held out his campaign as proof that in American democracy, energetic idealism could triumph over oceans of dark money.

"We're willing to do that thing that democracy is built on, which is having the conversations eye to eye with your neighbor about who we are and who we want to be, what we want for our America," he said. "You can't buy that. You can't buy inspiration. You can't buy people deciding to be a part of something. You can't buy hope."

You also can't buy the ability to entrance a crowd. "The thing about Abdul — beyond his charisma, which everyone knows about — is that he is so whip smart," said Jordan Acker, a lawyer deeply involved in Michigan Democratic politics. With many politicians, he said, there's a gap between their public and private selves, but El-Sayed is different. "What you see in private is who he is in public, and his ability to think on his feet is unlike any person I think I've ever met."

Acker's praise is striking because he voted for Stevens in the primary and isn't sure he's going to support El-Sayed in November, owing to their differences on Israel. The two men have known each other since 2004, and they have regularly discussed the Middle East over lunch. Acker doesn't think El-Sayed is an antisemite, nor does he think that his position on Israel is entirely unreasonable. El-Sayed says that he's fine with any sort of settlement, one state or two, that offers peace and self-determination to both Jews and Palestinians in the region. That's not far from where Acker himself stands.

What troubles Acker is a certain recklessness in El-Sayed's language: "His rhetoric, in my view, is more extreme than the candidate and the person underneath," he said. It's understandable that El-Sayed would rail against AIPAC, which has, after all, already spent tens of millions of dollars to defeat him. But Acker is disturbed by what he sees as El-Sayed's promotion of conspiratorial thinking about AIPAC as the source of many American ills. And he thinks El-Sayed has helped bring some toxic figures into the Democratic mainstream, notably Piker.

El-Sayed's embrace of Piker, who was with him again Monday, demonstrates how the candidate's mental model of the electorate differs from that of older political hands. For most political professionals, there's nothing to be gained from allying with someone so alienating to moderates. But if you believe on some level that most voters would see the wisdom of your message if only you could reach them, then collaborating with a figure such as Piker to capture voters' attention makes sense.

The surprisingly strong showing of Stevens — who made Piker a central part of her campaign — should lead El-Sayed to reconsider.

El-Sayed's basic political assumptions about the electorate are often shared by populists of both the right and the left. Both camps tend to assume that they represent "the people," and that if our politics don't reflect their views, it's because they're distorted by elites who use their influence to deny voters a clear choice. Often, they're wrong.

Consider the case that Phyllis Schlafly made for Barry Goldwater in her 1964 book, "A Choice Not an Echo." Cheering his ability to get things done without the help of Republican "kingmakers," she wrote, "Senator Goldwater gave us dramatic proof that conservatism is popular."

Goldwater's campaign helped incubate the right-wing movement that now dominates our country, so in the long term, you might consider it a success. But in 1964 he lost 44 states to Lyndon Johnson.

The Michigan Senate race, of course, isn't the only place where the populist left is trying to show it can win outside of Democratic strongholds. In the Lansing-area swing congressional district once held by Elissa Slotkin, who is now a centrist Democratic senator, the party chose activist William Lawrence, a founder of the environmentalist Sunrise Movement, as its standard-bearer. He ran a campaign based largely on opposition to data centers, aid to Israel and the war with Iran and will now take on Tom Barrett, the Republican incumbent in his first term.

And next week in Wisconsin, polls show democratic socialist Francesca Hong running away with the nomination for governor. Hong is a particularly stark example of the left-wing populist tendency to overestimate the popularity of its own positions. When I interviewed her earlier this year, I was unnerved by the way she either didn't see or wouldn't acknowledge that many of her views, regardless of their validity, are fairly marginal.

She didn't think that calls she once made to defund the police, which she doesn't disavow, would hurt her, because, she said, "a lot of people are losing trust in law enforcement, especially in the time of ICE." She thought that people in small towns and rural areas have a natural affinity for socialism because of the way neighbors took care of one another. "There is this element of mutual aid and community care that is a big part of democratic socialism, that we aren't always making that connection," she said.

This conversation has nagged at me because it suggested a refusal or inability to understand where people with competing perspectives are coming from. Neighborliness can coexist with lots of different political philosophies; conservatives abhor socialism precisely because they fear replacing community relationships with the state.

Democratic socialists are certainly wise to try to make inroads in new places by emphasizing common values. The mistake, I think, is assuming that people with good values will inevitably end up where you are if only they're shown the way.

This is not a trap that El-Sayed needs to fall into. He is extremely talented; Acker, despite his hesitations, thinks El-Sayed's dogged intelligence would probably make him a good senator. His cockiness has carried him far. Without it, he might never have been able to prevail over both Michigan's Democratic power structure and the tsunami of dark money spent to turn the state against him. But as he meets Michigan voters who aren't sold on the left, perhaps he could do with the smallest bit of doubt.
